use_case: Natural language processing to triage open-source scientific and technical literature for nuclear fuel-cycle relevance in safeguards evaluation
incurred_insecurity:
This NLP triage system introduces insecurity primarily through its role as an automated pre-filter in the IAEA's safeguards intelligence collection, where false negatives create persistent blind spots to proliferation-relevant technical developments published in open literature. An adversary aware of the system can evade it by crafting fuel-cycle research using linguistic patterns the classifier has not seen, or poison the open-source corpus with chaff or subtly biased papers to degrade triage accuracy and overwhelm human reviewers. The system also becomes a high-value counterintelligence target: compromise of its flagged-document queue, training data, or query logs reveals what the IAEA suspects and where inspectors will focus, while exfiltration or manipulation of the model itself allows an adversary to engineer systematic under-detection of specific proliferation pathways. Implicit weaknesses amplify these threats: the model's training distribution is static yet the adversary's publication strategy is adaptive, safeguards-relevant literature is scarce in the global scientific corpus, and automation bias leads analysts to trust the AI's relevance judgments without auditing its blind spots, converting a productivity tool into a single point of failure for open-source collection.

Adversarial Evasion and Corpus Manipulation
An adversary can study publicly available NLP models and embeddings to reverse-engineer what linguistic features the triage system keys on, then author or commission technical papers discussing sensitive fuel-cycle work using paraphrased terminology, synonym substitution, non-standard vocabulary, or novel journal venues the model has never encountered, causing the classifier to systematically miss proliferation-significant material. This is an adversarial threat exploiting the model's fixed training distribution. The adversary can also seed open repositories with poisoned datasets—plausible but misleading technical papers, or floods of chaff on irrelevant isotopes—to bias the model's learned concept of safeguards relevance or degrade precision to the point where human reviewers experience alarm fatigue and skip borderline cases. If the poisoned material enters the training corpus during retraining, the adversarial manipulation becomes persistent.

Counterintelligence Exfiltration and Insider Amplification
The system's classification decisions, flagged-document queues, and query patterns are high-value counterintelligence: an adversary who exfiltrates these learns what the IAEA suspects, which fuel-cycle signatures are under scrutiny, and which countries or facilities are investigative priorities. This is a pure adversarial threat via credential compromise, exploitation of public-facing interfaces, or supply-chain insertion of exfiltration logic. If the system includes generative summarization or an LLM-based query interface for analysts, prompt injection or jailbreak could exfiltrate the system prompt and reveal prioritized fuel-cycle keywords—a blueprint of what not to publish to evade safeguards. A malicious insider with lower-privilege access to this triage tool can observe or subtly manipulate the IAEA's information-gathering radar by tweaking model weights to suppress certain topics or leaking triage queues in near-real-time.

Training-Data Scarcity and Concept Drift
Safeguards-relevant literature is a tiny, evolving fraction of global scientific publishing, and truly novel proliferation pathways have scarce or zero training examples until they appear in the wild. This is an implicit vulnerability: the model will systematically under-detect emerging fuel-cycle techniques, new isotope-separation methods, alternative reprocessing chemistries, or additive manufacturing of fuel hardware because its training distribution does not cover them. Concept drift is guaranteed as the technical frontier moves and adversaries adopt new terminology or publish in underrepresented languages and venues. The model has no mechanism to flag its own uncertainty when encountering out-of-distribution text, so false negatives propagate silently. An adversary can exploit this implicit weakness by timing covert R&D to coincide with the model's blind spots, or by deliberately publishing in formats the model was never trained on.

Automation Bias and Lack of Explainability
If analysts come to trust the triage system and skim or skip papers scored as low-relevance, the AI converts from a productivity aid into a single point of failure for collection—the system does not fail loudly, it fails silently by not flagging what it should, and no human catches it because they have gone out-of-the-loop. This is an implicit human-factors vulnerability. The model's opacity makes it nearly impossible for analysts to understand why a borderline paper was excluded, so they cannot audit triage decisions or detect systematic blind spots an adversary has engineered via evasion or poisoning. Non-determinism in transformer-based inference means the same paper may be triaged differently depending on model version or inference parameters, eroding the reliability of the collection baseline and making it harder to diagnose when the model has drifted or been compromised.

Cross-Site Model Propagation and Supply-Chain Risk
If this classifier is shared across IAEA departments, member-state safeguards authorities, or regional offices, a single model defect, adversarial backdoor, or poisoned training update propagates across the entire open-source collection enterprise, creating a systemic blind spot. This is both an adversarial threat (supply-chain compromise of the model, training data, or software dependencies during development or deployment) and an implicit infrastructure vulnerability (lack of per-deployment qualification and insufficient retraining cadence to track evolving fuel-cycle terminology). Hosting the system on cloud infrastructure or off-IAEA premises introduces additional exfiltration and manipulation risk via third-party dependencies.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, this use case introduces insecurity primarily through **automation bias in an intelligence-collection context where false negatives are particularly costly**. If the AI triage under-flags relevant safeguards literature (e.g., dual-use fuel-cycle research, conversion or enrichment facility design evolution, reprocessing chemistry advances), analysts lose situational awareness of proliferation-relevant technical developments -- a gap an adversary can exploit by timing covert activities when the open-source watchlist has gone stale. The system's training data scarcity around **emerging or novel fuel-cycle techniques** (OP.C0701.02, OP.C0203) and the non-repeatability of transformer-based classifiers (OP.C0402.02) mean that the same paper could be triaged differently depending on model version or inference parameters, eroding the reliability of the collection baseline. Because this is a **pre-filter for human review rather than a direct facility control**, the consequence is slower or incomplete detection of safeguards-relevant technical trends, not an immediate plant-safety event -- but that intelligence gap degrades the IAEA's ability to identify undeclared activities or verify declared inventories, which is the safeguards mission.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** An adversary aware that the IAEA uses NLP triage can craft or seed open-source publications with **linguistic evasion** -- phrasing dual-use fuel-cycle work in benign process-engineering or materials-science vocabulary that the classifier has not seen or misclassifies (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model). They could also **poison or spam the open literature** with chaff papers (AML.T0046, AML.T0019 Publish Poisoned Datasets if they target the training corpus) to degrade classifier precision and overwhelm human reviewers, effectively blinding the collection system. Prompt-injection or model-extraction attacks (AML.T0051, AML.T0024.002) are lower risk here because the system likely operates as a batch classifier rather than an interactive LLM, but if the tooling uses generative summarization or translation (OP.C0304.02, OP.C0304.03), an adversary embedding instructions in a paper's abstract could manipulate downstream analysis. The larger attack surface is **supply-chain compromise of the NLP model or its training data** (AML.T0010.003 Data, AML.T0010.001 AI Software) -- if an adversary backdoors the model during development or fine-tuning, they can engineer systematic under-flagging of papers from specific institutions, authors, or technical keywords.

**Implicit (non-adversarial) insecurity:** The classifier's **data provenance and base-rate problem** (OP.C0201, OP.C0202) is acute: safeguards-relevant literature is a tiny fraction of global scientific publishing, and truly novel proliferation pathways (new centrifuge designs, alternative reprocessing chemistries, additive manufacturing of fuel hardware) have **scarce or zero training examples** until they appear in the wild (OP.C0203, OP.C0701.02). This guarantees **concept drift** (OP.C0302.02) as the technical frontier moves and the model's fuel-cycle ontology becomes outdated. **Automation bias** (OP.C0101.04 misuse, OP.C0102 complacency) is the killer: if analysts come to trust the triage and skim or skip papers the AI scored as low-relevance, the system converts from a productivity aid into a **single point of failure for collection**. Non-determinism in inference (OP.C0402.02) means the same paper may be flagged or missed depending on when it is processed, and the lack of explainability (OP.C0401) makes it nearly impossible for an analyst to understand *why* a borderline paper was excluded, so they cannot audit the triage decisions. Finally, **cross-site model propagation** (OP.C0602): if this classifier is deployed widely (e.g., shared among State support organizations or regional safeguards offices), a single model defect or adversarial manipulation propagates across the entire open-source collection enterprise, creating a systemic blind spot.

ai_engineer.argument: This is fundamentally a retrieval-oriented NLP system operating on continuously arriving public literature (journals, preprints, technical blogs) to surface fuel-cycle relevant documents for human analysts. My lens focuses on how the model was trained, what distribution it saw, and what happens when inference-time text diverges. The core vulnerability is that NukeLM and similar classifiers are trained on a snapshot of historical nuclear-literature language—terminology, document structure, authorship patterns—yet the adversary can intentionally craft publications using novel phrasing, obfuscated technical terms, or entirely new journal venues the model has never seen, causing the triage system to systematically miss proliferation-significant material. This is compounded by the operational reality: safeguards analysts depend on this system to pre-filter an enormous volume of open-source text, so concept drift (new fuel-cycle terminology, emerging isotope separation techniques described in non-standard language) or adversarial evasion (deliberate synonym substitution, paraphrasing to evade keyword/embedding match) directly translates to intelligence gaps—material goes undetected because the model's training distribution is static and the adversary's publication strategy is adaptive.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: From the ML engineering perspective, the dominant threat class is training-data staleness and adversarial transferability. NukeLM was trained on a corpus of known fuel-cycle literature, but an adversary can study publicly available NLP embeddings and document classifiers (ATLAS AML.T0000 series reconnaissance, AML.T0005 proxy-model training) to reverse-engineer what linguistic features the system keys on, then author or commission technical papers that discuss sensitive fuel-cycle R&D using paraphrased terminology, non-English-origin neologisms, or embedding-space perturbations invisible to human reviewers but sufficient to drop the document below the relevance threshold. The system architecture itself creates a single point of failure: if the triage model misclassifies a document as irrelevant, it never reaches the human analyst, and the safeguards gap persists undetected until much later (if ever). This is further exacerbated by the implicit operational vulnerabilities: the model has no mechanism to flag its own uncertainty when it encounters out-of-distribution text (OP.C0302 drift, OP.C0402 non-determinism in embedding space), the training pipeline likely did not include adversarially crafted evasion samples (OP.C0501 qualification gap for adversarial robustness), and there is no documented retraining cadence to capture emerging fuel-cycle terminology from new isotope-separation or reprocessing research published in languages or venues underrepresented in the original corpus (OP.C0302.01 data drift). An adversary does not need to hack the system—they only need to publish in a way that systematically exploits the distributional assumptions baked into the training data, and the safeguards workflow downstream inherits a blind spot. Additionally, if the model is shared across IAEA departments or member-state support programs (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation), a single evasion strategy propagates globally, and the false-negative rate becomes systemic rather than isolated. The security consequence is that proliferation-relevant technical progress becomes invisible to the safeguards regime precisely when it is being documented in open literature, because the NLP filter was never trained—and operationally cannot be retrained fast enough—to recognize the adversary's evolving linguistic strategy.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, this use case is a high-value intelligence target masquerading as a literature-triage tool. A sophisticated adversary (state or proxy) gains enormous strategic advantage by knowing which fuel-cycle activities the IAEA's safeguards analysts are searching for in open literature — that reveals where inspectors suspect undeclared activity, what technical signatures they're monitoring, and which countries or facilities are under scrutiny. The system itself becomes a sensor for adversary counterintelligence: compromise the model's query logs, training data, or flagged-document queue and you've effectively reverse-engineered the IAEA's investigative priorities. Beyond pure espionage, an adversary could poison the system's training corpus (injecting plausible but misleading technical papers into open repositories) to either bury genuine proliferation-relevant publications under noise or, more insidiously, train the model to miss specific fuel-cycle techniques the adversary intends to use — a long-game supply-chain attack on the safeguards knowledge base itself.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) The system's query patterns, flagged documents, and classification decisions are high-value counterintelligence — an adversary who exfiltrates these (AML.T0024 family, AML.T0057 LLM data leakage if the system uses generative components, or classic AML.T0025 exfiltration if they compromise the hosting infrastructure) learns what the IAEA suspects and where inspectors will look next. (2) Training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0019 publish poisoned datasets) is feasible because the system ingests open literature: an adversary seeds arXiv, technical blogs, or conference pre-prints with subtly misleading fuel-cycle research (e.g., papers that downplay detectability of certain reprocessing signatures, or flood the corpus with chaff on irrelevant isotopes) to bias NukeLM's learned concept of 'safeguards-relevant,' causing it to systematically under-flag real proliferation pathways (AML.T0031 erode model integrity, AML.T0015 evade model). (3) If the system has any LLM-based summarization or query interface for analysts, prompt injection (AML.T0051) or jailbreak (AML.T0054) could be used to exfiltrate the system prompt (AML.T0056), revealing the IAEA's prioritized fuel-cycle keywords and detection logic — a blueprint of what not to publish if you want to evade safeguards scrutiny. (4) Insider threat amplification: a malicious insider with access to this system (AML.T0012 valid accounts, likely lower-privilege than direct safeguards data access) can now observe or subtly manipulate the IAEA's information-gathering radar, either by tweaking model weights (AML.T0018 manipulate model) to suppress certain topics or by exfiltrating triage queues to tip off a proliferator in near-real-time.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) WEAKNESSES THAT CREATE OR EXACERBATE ADVERSARIAL SURFACE: (1) Data provenance brittleness (OP.C0201 category, OP.C0201.03 transferred/virtual data if pre-trained on non-nuclear corpora, OP.C0204 availability/continuity): if NukeLM was fine-tuned on a narrow safeguards literature set and now ingests the firehose of open publishing, it faces severe out-of-distribution risk (OP.C0302 drift family, OP.C0302.01 data/operational drift) — adversaries can exploit this by publishing in venues or formats the model wasn't trained on, causing it to miss new fuel-cycle research paradigms. (2) Safeguards-specific data scarcity (OP.C0701 family, especially OP.C0701.01 if the model must recognize undeclared reprocessing or enrichment signatures from sparse historical examples): an adversary knows the model likely has weak coverage of novel or less-common fuel-cycle pathways, so they can safely publish research on those techniques with low risk of IAEA flagging. (3) Automation bias and alarm fatigue (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust, OP.C0102 monitoring complacency): if analysts come to rely on the NLP triage and trust its 'not safeguards-relevant' labels, an adversary's poisoned or adversarially-crafted papers (designed to just barely miss the model's decision boundary) will be ignored by human reviewers who've gone out-of-the-loop (OP.C0101.01) — the system doesn't fail loudly, it fails silently by not flagging what it should, and no human catches it. (4) Model opacity (OP.C0401 explainability limit): if analysts can't easily audit why the model flagged or didn't flag a paper, they can't detect systematic blind spots an adversary has engineered via poisoning, nor can they verify the model isn't drifting (OP.C0302) as the publication landscape evolves — this makes the system a persistent, unauditable single point of failure in the IAEA's information supply chain. (5) Cross-agency/cloud inference risk (OP.C0601 if hosted off-IAEA premises, OP.C0602 if the model is shared across IAEA departments or with member-state safeguards authorities): compromise of the shared model or its hosting infrastructure (AML.T0010 supply chain, AML.T0049 exploit public-facing application if there's a web interface) propagates poisoned triage logic to all downstream users, and an adversary gains a single choke-point to monitor or manipulate the entire safeguards community's open-source research awareness.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on adversarial evasion via linguistic crafting, training-data poisoning of the open corpus, automation bias leading to silent false-negative propagation, and concept drift from scarce safeguards-relevant training examples; the security specialist's counterintelligence exfiltration angle and supply-chain propagation risk were accepted as genuinely distinct adversarial dimensions the other two implied but did not fully articulate.

evidence.note: ORNL/BNL/PNNL demonstration of NLP tools, including NukeLM text classification, for the IAEA's largely manual open-source collection workflow.

damage.why: Systematic blind spots in safeguards open-source intelligence collection can enable undetected proliferation pathway development and undermine material accountancy verification, directly threatening nuclear material control and safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Adversarial evasion via linguistic manipulation and training-data scarcity causing false negatives are highly reproducible once the adversary understands the model's feature space or exploits known out-of-distribution weaknesses in NLP classifiers.

exploitability.why: Linguistic evasion requires only publication access and understanding of NLP embeddings (often reverse-engineerable from public models), while corpus poisoning can be achieved by seeding open repositories without insider access to IAEA systems.

affected_users.why: The vulnerability affects the entire safeguards intelligence collection enterprise and propagates across IAEA departments, member-state authorities, and regional offices if the model is shared, creating systemic blind spots.

discoverability.why: The existence of NLP triage systems for safeguards literature is documented in public ORNL/BNL/PNNL presentations to INMM, and general weaknesses of NLP classifiers to adversarial evasion and training-distribution limitations are well-known in open AI security literature.

use_case: Deep-learning detection of spent fuel cask movements in safeguards surveillance imagery
incurred_insecurity:
This use case introduces a concentrated vulnerability at the intersection of small-dataset machine learning and high-consequence safeguards verification. The deep-learning detection model, trained on imagery from only 23 cameras across five facilities, must generalize to diverse and evolving operational conditions—new camera placements, cask designs, lighting regimes, facility modifications—that fall outside its narrow training envelope. When the model fails to detect a cask movement, either through implicit drift or adversarial evasion, the safeguards chain breaks: inspectors relying on automated pre-screening may never review the critical frames, and a diversion opportunity opens undetected. The remote transmission architecture and integration into fleet-wide review software amplify both adversarial and implicit risks, as a single compromised model version or a systematically exploited training gap can propagate across multiple facilities, eroding the IAEA's material accountability posture at scale.

Training-Data Scarcity and Operational Drift
The model's training corpus—23 cameras, five sites—is insufficient to capture the full operational diversity of spent-fuel handling worldwide. New facilities, retrofitted camera systems, seasonal lighting changes, introduction of next-generation cask geometries, or even temporary obstructions (scaffolding, weather) push the model out-of-distribution, causing false negatives (missed detections) that safeguards inspectors depend on to maintain continuity of knowledge. This is an implicit weakness rooted in the small-data problem and the low base rate of actual diversion events, meaning the model's performance under adversarial or novel conditions remains uncharacterized. If the model drifts without retraining as facilities evolve, detection confidence degrades silently, and material movements go unrecorded until a discrepancy surfaces—potentially months later.

Adversarial Evasion and Supply-Chain Manipulation
An adversary aware of the model's training distribution and deployment architecture can exploit its generalization limits through physical manipulation of the surveillance environment or injection of crafted data into the imagery pipeline. Manual modification of the scene—partial camera occlusion, timing movements during atypical lighting, introducing visually similar decoy objects—can suppress detection confidence below the threshold for human review, effectively evading the AI system. More sophisticated actors may poison the training data during model updates, compromise the data supply chain (cameras, transmission infrastructure, or the review software integration layer), or craft adversarial perturbations tailored to the model's learned features, all aiming to mask a cask removal without triggering an alarm. Because the model outputs feed directly into the Next Generation Surveillance Review software used across multiple facilities, a successful attack or a systematically exploitable weakness propagates fleet-wide, allowing an adversary to time diversions to periods of known model uncertainty at scale.

Automation Bias and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Risk
As inspectors grow accustomed to the system reliably flagging movements, they may reduce manual scrutiny of raw imagery, trusting negative detections (no flag = no movement) and deprioritizing review of ambiguous or low-confidence frames. This automation complacency means that when the model does fail—whether from drift, adversarial evasion, or a scenario outside its training envelope—the failure is less likely to be caught by human oversight, and the safeguards authority's assurance erodes without immediate awareness. Over time, inspectors may lose the practiced skill to spot subtle anomalies in surveillance footage, compounding the risk when the AI is absent or compromised. The model's lack of explainability further hinders inspectors' ability to challenge or corroborate its outputs with independent judgment, a particular liability in safeguards where accountability decisions must be legally and technically defensible.

Cross-Site Model Propagation and Regulatory Qualification Gaps
Deploying a common detection model or architecture across the IAEA's safeguards surveillance fleet creates a common-mode vulnerability: a systematic flaw, adversarial backdoor, or training-data bias becomes a shared weakness at multiple facilities simultaneously. If a poisoned model version is pushed during an update cycle, or if an adversary reverse-engineers the detection logic from one site and applies evasion techniques elsewhere, the impact scales beyond a single facility. The lack of established verification and validation standards for safeguards ML systems means the model's qualification envelope, acceptable drift thresholds, and procedures for retraining or rollback are ad hoc, leaving the IAEA without a clear framework to assess when the system's assurance value has degraded to the point of requiring human-only review or facility-specific requalification.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case sits squarely in the safeguards domain where the AI output directly informs accountability decisions -- whether spent fuel has moved, when, and whether movement was declared. From an operational and safeguards lens, the consequence of missed detection (false negative) is a potential diversion opportunity undetected, while false positives burden inspectors with review workload and erode trust in the system. The training data comes from only 23 cameras across five facilities, raising immediate questions about generalization to new facility lighting, camera angles, cask designs, or environmental conditions not in that set. If the model drifts or fails on a sixth facility's imagery, or if an adversary understands what visual features the model keys on, the entire safeguards surveillance chain weakens at a critical chokepoint -- the human reviewer may never see the anomaly flagged, or may dismiss legitimate flags as algorithm noise.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The central threat is **data scarcity and operational drift** (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0203): 23 cameras from five facilities is a narrow training envelope for a task meant to generalize across diverse spent-fuel storage sites, transport configurations, lighting regimes, and cask geometries worldwide. A new facility with different camera placement, a next-generation cask design, or even seasonal lighting changes may push the model out-of-distribution, causing missed detections that safeguards inspectors rely on to maintain continuity of knowledge. This is compounded by **automation complacency** (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): if the AI flags most movements correctly for months, inspectors may stop scrutinizing borderline or ambiguous frames, so when the model does fail -- due to drift or adversarial manipulation -- the failure goes unnoticed until material is already diverted. 

On the adversarial side, an informed adversary could exploit the narrow training set via **physical environment manipulation** (AML.T0041) or **craft adversarial data** at the camera input (AML.T0043.003 manual modification, e.g., partial occlusion, decoy objects, or non-standard movement paths not in the training corpus). Because the model's detection likely keys on shape, motion vectors, or scene context learned from those 23 cameras, an attacker with knowledge of the facility and model deployment could time a covert cask movement during conditions (weather, time of day, partial camera obstruction) that the model was never trained to handle, effectively **evading the AI** (AML.T0015). If the surveillance review software auto-flags only high-confidence detections, a near-threshold evasion may never surface for human review, breaking the safeguards chain. 

Additionally, there is **fleet-wide propagation risk** (OP.C0602): if the same model or a common architecture is deployed across multiple IAEA-monitored sites, a systematic flaw (e.g., sensitivity to a particular occlusion pattern) becomes a common-mode vulnerability -- an adversary can test evasion techniques at one site and apply them elsewhere. The integration into Next Generation Surveillance Review software also introduces **skill fade and out-of-the-loop risk** (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06): inspectors who rely on AI pre-screening may lose the practiced eye for subtle anomalies in raw footage, making them less effective when the AI fails or is absent. Finally, **explainability limits** (OP.C0401) mean that when the model does or does not flag a movement, the inspector has little insight into *why*, hindering their ability to challenge or corroborate the output with independent judgment -- a particular problem in safeguards where accountability decisions must be legally and technically defensible.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case runs a CNN (YOLOv3) on remotely transmitted surveillance imagery from actual safeguards cameras at operating facilities to detect spent fuel cask movements. The model was trained on images from 23 cameras across five facilities—a dataset that is necessarily small, operationally heterogeneous (different camera positions, lighting, cask geometries, facility layouts), and drawn from a handful of real-world sites with no public analogue for pretraining or transfer learning. Because this is safeguards verification, the failure mode is not just missing a cask in the feed but an adversary timing a diversion or substitution event to periods when the model's detection confidence degrades—exploiting lighting changes, camera obstructions, or previously unseen cask configurations that the small training set never captured. The pipeline architecture (remote transmission → model inference → integration into review software) means that data freshness, transmission integrity, and the non-determinism of the CNN at inference time all become attack or failure surfaces with direct consequences for treaty compliance and proliferation risk.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core ML vulnerability is training-data scarcity compounded by operational heterogeneity: 23 cameras across five facilities yields a dataset far too small to generalize robustly to new camera placements, facility modifications, seasonal lighting variation, or adversarial occlusion (e.g., temporary scaffolding, fog, intentional glare). An adversary aware of the model's training distribution can craft scenarios—moving a cask during atypical lighting, partially occluding the camera's field of view, or introducing a visually similar decoy object—that fall outside the model's training envelope and produce false negatives (missed detections) or false positives (review fatigue leading to automation complacency). The remote-transmission architecture introduces supply-chain and data-integrity risks: an adversary with access to the camera feed or transmission pathway can inject adversarially perturbed frames (AML.T0043 crafted adversarial data, AML.T0015 evade model), poison the imagery to degrade detection over time (AML.T0020), or manipulate metadata timestamps to desynchronize cask movement records with actual events. Because the model outputs are integrated into a review tool used by human inspectors, automation bias (OP.C0101.04 over-trust) is a significant risk—if the model consistently shows 'no movement detected,' inspectors may reduce manual scrutiny, and a real diversion event during a model failure or adversarial evasion window goes unnoticed. The non-determinism of deep learning inference (OP.C0402.02) means identical imagery may yield slightly different bounding-box confidences or missed detections across runs, complicating forensic replay if a safeguards discrepancy is later suspected. Finally, the qualification and regulatory framework for this system is unclear: safeguards ML models lack established V&V standards (OP.C0501), and if the model drifts due to facility changes (new lighting, camera repositioning, introduction of new cask designs) without retraining (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03), the IAEA's confidence in the system erodes but may not be discovered until after a material-unaccounted-for event. The fact that this is safeguards—not safety—means the adversary's objective is to evade detection entirely, and the model's small-data foundation, lack of adversarial hardening, and integration into a remote-review workflow collectively open a window for undetected diversion if an adversary can time their action to periods of model uncertainty or successfully inject crafted imagery into the feed.

security_specialist.argument: This use case fundamentally alters the safeguards assurance chain by automating what was previously direct human observation of accountable nuclear material movements. From a security perspective, the primary concern is that an adversary who can compromise the AI detection pipeline—whether through training-data poisoning at the limited-facility scale (23 cameras, five sites), adversarial perturbations to live imagery, or supply-chain insertion into the detection model or Next Generation Surveillance Review integration layer—gains the ability to mask cask movements or inject phantom detections at scale across multiple facilities. The remote transmission architecture and centralized review software create a high-value target: compromise here affects fleet-wide material accountability rather than a single site. Even absent a sophisticated attack, the system's reliance on training data from a small number of facilities (concept drift, operational heterogeneity) and the low base rate of actual diversion events mean the model's false-negative rate in adversarial or novel scenarios is essentially uncharacterized, and inspectors may have already begun trusting the system's negative calls enough that a deliberate evasion would go unnoticed longer than under the old manual-review regime.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core threat is **adversarial manipulation enabling undetected diversion**. An insider or remote attacker who can inject adversarial perturbations into transmitted imagery, poison the training set during model updates, or exploit the integration seam between detection output and the Next Generation Surveillance Review software can cause the system to fail to flag a cask removal or movement—allowing diversion of spent fuel without alarm. The remote transmission and centralized processing model (AML.T0010.003 data supply chain, AML.T0020 training data poisoning, AML.T0043 adversarial-data crafting) mean an adversary need not be physically present at the facility during the diversion; they can pre-position the attack in the model or imagery pipeline. The small training corpus (five facilities, 23 cameras) makes the model especially vulnerable to targeted evasion: an adversary with knowledge of even one facility's camera angles and cask-handling procedures can craft realistic operational scenarios the model has never seen, exploiting the generalization gap (OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity, OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity if extended to new facilities). **Automation bias and alarm complacency** (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust, OP.C0102) are the second-order threat: if inspectors or the safeguards authority come to rely on the system's negative detections (no movement flagged = no movement occurred), the human verification loop erodes, and the system becomes a single point of failure. An adversary can time a diversion to coincide with a period of known model drift, a facility configuration change, or simply a scenario outside the training distribution, confident that the miss will be attributed to a benign model limitation rather than investigated as potential evasion. The **cross-site model propagation** (OP.C0602) is also a force-multiplier: if a poisoned or evadable model version is pushed to the fleet, the adversary's capability scales across all facilities using the system, and the IAEA's assurance posture degrades globally rather than at one site.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on training-data scarcity, operational drift, adversarial evasion via crafted data or physical manipulation, automation bias, and cross-site propagation risk as the main threats. Disagreements were minor and stylistic; the security specialist emphasized supply-chain entry points more explicitly, while the AI engineer detailed inference non-determinism, but these map to the same underlying vulnerabilities and were integrated without conflict.

use_case: Computer-vision detection of malicious acts in security camera video at nuclear power plants
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places an AI-driven detection system at the front line of physical security, where failure to detect a genuine intrusion (false negative) or flooding operators with nuisance alarms (false positive) directly degrades the facility's protection posture. Because actual malicious acts at NPPs are vanishingly rare, the AI is trained predominantly on simulated intrusions, synthetic adversary behaviors, and authorized personnel activity, creating a structural vulnerability to adversaries who craft tactics outside the training distribution. An attacker who understands the model—through reconnaissance, insider access, or proxy training—can evade detection by exploiting blind spots in the sensor fusion, timing intrusions during high false-alarm periods, or poisoning the training data to suppress specific threat signatures. Even without adversarial action, the system's reliance on small-data training, operational drift, and non-deterministic inference erodes operator trust over time, and the automation complacency this induces becomes an exploitable vulnerability: adversaries time attacks when guards have learned to discount AI alerts as noise, effectively weaponizing the system's own false-positive history.

Adversarial Evasion and Reconnaissance
An adversary who learns the detection model's training set or decision boundaries—via reconnaissance of camera fields of view, active scanning of sensor layouts, or extraction of model parameters—can craft physical evasion tactics such as unusual gait, occlusion behind objects, or timing intrusions during environmental conditions (weather, wildlife activity) that the model associates with nuisance alarms. This is a direct adversarial attack on the AI's inference process, exploiting the fact that the model was never trained on determined adversary tradecraft, only on benign motion and staged red-team exercises. The attacker may also deploy physical adversarial examples (clothing patterns, movement styles) that the vision model misclassifies as authorized personnel.

Training Data and Model Poisoning
If an adversary gains access to the training pipeline—through supply-chain compromise of data sources, insider action, or network intrusion into the model management system—they can inject mislabeled examples that teach the model to ignore specific threat vectors. For instance, genuine intrusion attempts labeled as 'nuisance wildlife' or 'authorized maintenance' degrade the model's sensitivity to those signatures in future deployments. This is an adversarial manipulation of the AI's learning process. Similarly, a compromised model artifact pushed via supply-chain or insider channels can embed backdoor triggers that selectively suppress alarms when a specific visual or radar cue appears, giving the attacker a 'green light' window.

Denial of Service and Resource Exhaustion
The system's real-time inference workload and operator attention span are both finite resources. An adversary can flood the perimeter with coordinated nuisance activity—drones, reflective objects, simultaneous motion at multiple sensor zones—to exhaust computational capacity, overwhelm the fusion analytics, or trigger so many alarms that human analysts cannot triage them effectively. This creates a window where a real intrusion goes unnoticed amid the noise. This is an adversarial attack on the AI's availability and the human-AI decision loop.

Small-Data and Low Base-Rate Training
Genuine malicious acts at NPPs are extraordinarily rare, so the model is trained overwhelmingly on simulated intrusions, synthetic adversary behaviors, or data transferred from non-nuclear contexts. This creates an implicit vulnerability: the model has never seen a real, coordinated attack by a determined adversary and cannot reliably generalize to novel tactics, tools, or multi-vector entries. An adversary who studies public red-team exercises or insider knowledge of the training scenarios can choose an approach outside the learned distribution, confident the AI will fail to flag it. This is an implicit weakness in the AI's training data provenance and generalization capacity, which adversaries can exploit without directly attacking the model.

Operational Drift and Environmental Generalization
The detection system must generalize across changing lighting, weather, camera angles, facility construction, and evolving adversary tactics. If the model drifts out of calibration due to facility modifications (new buildings, camera repositioning), seasonal environmental changes (vegetation growth, snow cover), or shifts in authorized personnel patterns (shift changes, contractor access), its detection accuracy degrades. An adversary who surveils the site over time can identify these blind spots and time an intrusion accordingly. This is an implicit weakness in the AI's ability to handle operational heterogeneity, which adversaries exploit by choosing attack conditions outside the model's experience.

Automation Complacency and Alarm Fatigue
High false-positive rates—inevitable given the low base rate of true threats and the need for high sensitivity—train operators to discount AI-flagged events as noise. Over time, guards grow less vigilant in manual review, trust the AI's 'all clear' signals too readily, and lose familiarity with baseline threat signatures. An adversary who understands this dynamic (through insider knowledge or observation of guard response times) can time an intrusion during periods of known high nuisance-alarm activity (migratory wildlife, storms) when analyst fatigue peaks. This is an implicit human-factors vulnerability induced by the AI system, which adversaries exploit by choosing the timing and context of their attack.

Model Opacity and Non-Determinism
When the AI flags or fails to flag an event, operators cannot easily determine why, due to the model's complexity and lack of explainability. If the system uses non-deterministic inference (ensemble models, stochastic feature extraction), the same input may yield different outputs on repeated runs, complicating forensic review and making it impossible to qualify performance bounds. This opacity prevents operators from learning when to override the AI's judgment and leaves security planners uncertain whether a missed detection was adversarial evasion, model variability, or benign drift. This is an implicit limitation of the AI's transparency, which both degrades human override capability and hinders post-incident analysis.

Cross-Site Model Propagation
If the same AI model or centralized training pipeline is deployed across multiple NPPs, a single successful poisoning attack, discovered evasion technique, or compromised model update can undermine physical security at all sites simultaneously. An adversary who compromises the model supply chain or retraining infrastructure gains a 'one-to-many' capability, amplifying the impact of a single intrusion into the AI system. This is an implicit architectural vulnerability in fleet-wide AI deployment, which adversaries can exploit by targeting shared infrastructure.

Governance and Qualification Gaps
There is no established regulatory framework for qualifying AI-based physical security systems in the nuclear sector, so facilities may deploy models without validation against adversarial attacks, stress-testing under rare conditions, or formal integration with the design-basis threat response chain. This governance gap means security leadership cannot confidently assess whether the AI improves or degrades the overall protection posture, and adversaries benefit from the resulting uncertainty and lack of red-teaming. This is an implicit weakness in the regulatory and qualification process, not the AI itself, but it exacerbates all other vulnerabilities.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case sits in a critical trust boundary: security operators must decide whether AI-flagged behavior warrants a response (dispatch force, lockdown area, alarm facility leadership) or represents a false alarm. Unlike condition monitoring where physics provides a backstop, here the AI's judgment IS the early detection layer -- if it misses real malicious acts (false negatives) or floods operators with nuisance detections (false positives), the physical security posture degrades directly. The system fuses video and radar across multiple sensors and applies 'deliberate motion analytics,' so it depends on calibration, scene understanding, and distinguishing adversary from authorized personnel or environmental motion -- all areas where model drift, training-data limitations, and adversarial manipulation intersect. An adversary who knows the model exists can probe its detection threshold (e.g., slow approach, occlusion tactics, presentation attacks against cameras) or poison the model if they gain access to training pipelines or live sensor feeds, while non-adversarial failure modes (weather-induced false alarms, shift in facility foot-traffic patterns, sensor degradation) can erode operator trust and create windows where real intrusions go unnoticed.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) An insider or external attacker who understands the AI detection model can craft evasion techniques -- unusual gait, occlusion by objects, timing intrusion during high nuisance-alarm periods (weather, wildlife) -- to avoid triggering video-based alerts, effectively rendering the AI blind to deliberate malicious motion (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model, AML.T0043 Craft Adversarial Data). (2) If the attacker gains access to the video feed or the training pipeline (via supply chain, network intrusion, or insider action), they can inject poisoned data or manipulate the model to ignore specific patterns of motion or attire, creating blind spots for future intrusions (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0018.000 Poison AI Model). (3) The system's reliance on fused radar/video and real-time inference via cloud or on-premises infrastructure creates a denial-of-service surface: an adversary can flood the system with synthetic or replayed video, overwhelm processing capacity, or sever network links to delay alerts during an actual intrusion (AML.T0029 Denial of AI Service, AML.T0034 Cost Harvesting, AML.T0046 Spamming with Chaff Data). (4) If the AI system is networked or uses remote model updates, supply-chain compromise of model artifacts, container registries, or software dependencies can embed backdoors that selectively suppress alarms for certain scenarios (AML.T0010 AI Supply Chain Compromise).

IMPLICIT / NON-ADVERSARIAL THREATS (exploitable by adversaries): (5) The small-data problem for actual malicious acts is severe -- NPPs rarely experience genuine intrusions, so the model trains predominantly on simulated scenarios, authorized personnel motion, and nuisance alarms (wildlife, weather), creating a concept-drift and out-of-distribution risk when a real, novel attack occurs (OP.C0202 Small-data/low base-rate problem, OP.C0201.01/02 Simulated/synthetic data provenance, OP.C0302.02 Concept Drift). An adversary can time an intrusion to exploit this gap, knowing the model has never seen a real coordinated attack. (6) Automation-bias and alarm fatigue from false positives will lead operators to discount or delay response to AI alerts, especially if the system initially over-triggers on benign activity (shift changes, contractor access, environmental motion); an adversary can exploit this degraded trust by launching a real intrusion after priming the system with nuisance behavior (OP.C0101.04 Misuse/over-trust transitioning to OP.C0101.05 Disuse/under-trust, OP.C0102 Alarm/monitoring complacency). (7) The model's ability to generalize across lighting, weather, camera angles, and facility layout changes is unproven in live operation; concept drift from facility modifications (new construction, camera repositioning, changed access patterns post-outage) or environmental conditions not in training data can degrade detection accuracy, and an adversary who surveys the site can identify these blind spots (OP.C0302.01 Data/operational drift, OP.C0302.03 Operational heterogeneity). (8) If the system uses non-deterministic inference (e.g., ensemble models, stochastic feature extraction), the lack of repeatability complicates forensic review after an incident and makes it harder to qualify the system's performance bounds, leaving security planners uncertain whether a missed detection was adversarial evasion or model variability (OP.C0402.02 Inference-time non-repeatability). (9) Cross-site model propagation: if the same AI model or training pipeline is deployed across multiple NPPs, a single successful poisoning attack or discovered evasion technique can compromise physical security at all sites simultaneously (OP.C0602 Cross-site/fleet model propagation). (10) Governance and qualification gaps: there is no established regulatory framework for qualifying AI-based physical security systems in the nuclear sector, so facilities may deploy models without validation against adversarial attacks, stress-testing under rare conditions, or formal integration with the security plan's graded protection strategy (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA/qualification gap, OP.C0503 Threat-landscape/regulatory-scope drift). This leaves security leadership unable to confidently place the AI in the design-basis threat response chain.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case deploys computer vision for security threat detection in a live operational environment where the consequences of both false negatives (missed intrusions) and false positives (alarm fatigue leading to complacency) are severe. From an ML engineering standpoint, the core fragility is in the training data: malicious acts are rare events, so the model is trained predominantly on simulated intrusions, synthetic adversary behaviors, or transferred data from non-nuclear contexts—none of which may faithfully represent a determined adversary's actual tactics at a live NPP. At inference time, the system faces operational drift (lighting changes, weather, camera degradation, evolving adversary techniques) and must generalize to threat signatures it has never seen, a classic out-of-distribution failure mode. The fusion architecture (radar + video) introduces additional brittleness: if the models are trained and validated separately or on mismatched data streams, integration-time failures or mode confusion can occur, and the system's opacity makes it hard for security staff to know when to trust an alert versus override it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary ML-specific insecurity is the small-data / low base-rate problem for malicious acts: genuine intrusions and insider threats are vanishingly rare in NPP operational data, so training relies on simulated scenarios, red-team exercises, or data transferred from other facilities or domains (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01/.02/.03). An adversary aware of this can craft an intrusion that deviates from the simulated threat library—exploiting the model's inability to generalize to novel tactics (OP.C0302.01/.02)—and the system will fail to flag the event (false negative). Conversely, the model may be tuned to high sensitivity to compensate for data scarcity, generating frequent nuisance alarms that condition operators to disregard alerts (OP.C0101.04 misuse / OP.C0102 complacency), effectively disabling the detection capability when a real threat occurs. The adversarial surface is also present: an attacker with reconnaissance access to the camera field of view or knowledge of the model's training set (AML.T0000 series, AML.T0006) can craft evasion techniques—unusual gait, occlusion, timing—that the vision model was never trained to recognize (AML.T0015, AML.T0043 adversarial data crafting). The fusion of radar and video adds a non-determinism risk (OP.C0402.02): if the models produce inconsistent outputs under the same conditions due to inference-time variability or lack of synchronized retraining, operators may lose confidence in the system. Finally, because the model is likely retrained or updated periodically with new threat intelligence, there is a risk of cascading propagation (OP.C0602) if a compromised or poisoned model update is pushed across multiple NPP sites, undermining physical security fleetwide (AML.T0018.000 poison model, AML.T0010.003 supply chain via model).

security_specialist.argument: From a security specialist lens, this use case is a high-value target for adversaries because it sits at the chokepoint of threat detection—compromise here doesn't just mean the AI fails, it means the adversary controls what the facility *sees*. An attacker who can manipulate detection thresholds, poison training data with benign examples of malicious behavior, or exploit the system's reliance on fused radar-video correlation gains a timing advantage: they know when guards are trusting the AI and when nuisance-alarm fatigue has set in. The system also creates insider-threat surface: anyone with access to model retraining pipelines, video preprocessing, or alarm-tuning parameters can subtly degrade detection of specific threat profiles (e.g., a particular gait, tool signature, or entry vector) without tripping traditional access controls. Even non-adversarially, automation complacency and alarm fatigue are exactly what a sophisticated adversary would wait for or engineer—if operators learn to dismiss AI-flagged events as noise, the adversary effectively gets a 'green light' window, and the AI's existence has made the facility *less* secure than a human-only baseline with consistent vigilance.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: AML.T0043 (Craft Adversarial Data): An attacker with knowledge of the detection model (obtained via AML.T0024.002 model extraction or AML.T0005 proxy training on publicly available NPP perimeter datasets) crafts physical or digital adversarial examples—clothing patterns, movement styles, or video preprocessing manipulations—that evade detection while appearing benign to human review. AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data) and AML.T0010.002 (AI Supply Chain Compromise - Data): An insider or supply-chain attacker injects mislabeled training examples (e.g., marking genuine intrusion attempts as 'nuisance wildlife' or 'authorized maintenance') during model retraining, systematically degrading sensitivity to specific threat vectors the adversary intends to exploit. AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model): The adversary conducts reconnaissance (AML.T0006 Active Scanning, AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology) to learn detection blind spots (e.g., camera occlusion zones, radar-video fusion failure modes at certain ranges or weather conditions) and times the attack accordingly. AML.T0029 (Denial of AI Service): A distributed physical or cyber attack floods the system with coordinated nuisance alarms (e.g., AML.T0046 chaff—drones, reflective objects) to exhaust computational resources or analyst attention, creating a window where real intrusion goes undetected. AML.T0012 (Valid Accounts) + AML.T0018.000 (Poison AI Model): An insider with legitimate access to the security operations center or model management system subtly adjusts detection thresholds, whitelists certain behavioral signatures, or embeds a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) that suppresses alarms when a specific visual or radar cue is present (e.g., a particular RFID tag frequency or clothing pattern the insider shares with the external attacker).

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) INSECURITY THAT ADVERSARIES EXPLOIT: OP.C0101.04 (Automation Misuse/Over-Trust): Operators grow to trust AI-flagged events as the 'real' threats and dismiss non-flagged activity, even if contextually suspicious; an adversary who has studied the system's false-negative patterns (via AML.T0062-style probing or insider knowledge) exploits this trust window. OP.C0101.01 (Out-of-the-Loop Unfamiliarity): As the AI handles routine perimeter monitoring, human guards lose familiarity with baseline threat signatures and slower manual review skills—if the AI fails (adversarially or naturally), response time degrades. OP.C0102 (Alarm/Monitoring Complacency): Nuisance alarms (wildlife, weather, equipment vibration) that the AI cannot perfectly filter train operators to expect frequent false positives; adversaries time attacks during periods of known high false-alarm rates (e.g., migratory season, storm conditions) when analyst fatigue peaks. OP.C0302.01 (Data/Operational Drift): The system is trained on historical perimeter activity but faces novel threat tactics (e.g., drone-delivered tools, coordinated multi-vector entries) or environmental changes (new construction, vegetation growth altering camera fields of view) that the model was never exposed to—adversaries deliberately choose tactics outside the training distribution. OP.C0203 (New-Build Data Scarcity) and OP.C0202 (Low Base-Rate Problem): Genuine intrusion attempts at NPPs are rare, meaning the model is trained overwhelmingly on benign or staged data (OP.C0201.01 simulated, OP.C0201.02 synthetic); adversaries exploit the gap between synthetic training scenarios and real-world attack tradecraft. OP.C0401 (Explainability/Opacity Limit): When the AI flags (or doesn't flag) an event, operators cannot easily determine *why*—this blocks effective human override during ambiguous cases and prevents learning from near-misses, leaving adversaries' reconnaissance probes undetected if they don't cross the AI's learned threshold. OP.C0601 (Cloud/Off-Premises Dependency): If video preprocessing, model inference, or fusion analytics rely on cloud infrastructure (common for DNN workloads), adversaries gain additional attack surface via supply-chain or credential compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0055) outside the physical security perimeter. OP.C0602 (Cross-Site/Fleet Model Propagation): A single compromised model update (AML.T0018.000 poisoning or AML.T0010.003 model supply chain) propagates across multiple NPP sites if they share a centralized detection system, enabling a 'one-to-many' adversarial campaign.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the core threat: adversaries evading detection by exploiting training-data scarcity (simulated threats) and crafting tactics outside the learned distribution, plus the automation-complacency risk from false positives enabling timed attacks. The nuclear engineer emphasized regulatory qualification gaps and cross-site propagation; the AI engineer focused on ML-specific drift and non-determinism; the security specialist detailed insider/supply-chain poisoning and the weaponization of alarm fatigue. I unified these as distinct threat paragraphs under a common framework, assigning ATLAS codes only where an adversary actively manipulates the AI, and OP codes to implicit weaknesses adversaries exploit.
