evidence.note: Uses the NPP control system as a case study of process changes from faults versus cyber-attacks that can look alike to ML detectors.

damage.why: A missed intrusion leaves an adversary embedded in the control system with potential access to safety-critical functions, while false alarms during genuine equipment failures could delay appropriate maintenance response, both pathways risking operational safety margins or worse.

reproducibility.why: An adversary with knowledge of the model's training-data limitations (simulated attacks, fault-signature catalog) can reliably craft attacks mimicking learned fault patterns, as the model's decision boundary is constrained by its training distribution.

exploitability.why: Requires moderate insider knowledge or reconnaissance to understand which fault signatures the model has learned to dismiss, plus control-system access to inject crafted intrusion traffic, but does not require deep system internals or nation-state-only capabilities.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide deployment creates propagation risk where a compromised model or poisoned update degrades intrusion detection across multiple plants simultaneously, and successful evasion enables adversary persistence in control systems.

discoverability.why: The fundamental training-data scarcity problem for NPP control-system intrusions is documented in open literature (cited sources), making the reliance on simulated data and resulting model limitations inferable by capable adversaries without insider access to this specific deployment.

use_case: Nuclear-domain large language model continually pre-trained on internal technical reports to summarise institutional technical documentation
incurred_insecurity:
This system concentrates institutional knowledge from multiple fuel-cycle facilities into a single queryable artifact, creating both a high-value intelligence target and a multi-domain failure point. Adversaries with query access can extract compartmented technical details via prompt injection or membership inference, bypassing physical and role-based document controls. Insiders or supply-chain attackers can poison the training corpus with subtly incorrect procedures that propagate across enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and power operations, while the model's hallucinations and content-misattribution failures can mislead operators into unsafe actions without adversarial intent. The on-premise deployment, driven by security policy, paradoxically weakens operational security by limiting MLOps rigor, drift monitoring, and adversarial robustness testing, and the system erodes need-to-know discipline because users query across facility boundaries the model does not enforce.

Adversarial Exfiltration and Knowledge Concentration

An adversary with legitimate or compromised credentials can use the model as a cross-facility intelligence oracle, extracting technical details from domains they would never physically access—for example, an enrichment-site insider querying reprocessing material balances or fuel-fabrication criticality limits. Prompt injection (direct user queries or indirect via poisoned documents later ingested) can compel the model to leak safeguards-sensitive content such as cascade configurations, material accountancy procedures, or equipment specifications, effectively bypassing document-access controls that segregate operational knowledge. Membership inference and model inversion attacks allow iterative reconstruction of the ~4,000-report training corpus without ever touching the original document repository, and exfiltration of the fine-tuned model weights yields a pre-digested intelligence product far more valuable than piecemeal document theft. The system also enables reconnaissance at scale: an adversary can rapidly prototype plausible technical scenarios or identify procedural gaps by querying institutional norms and jargon across all fuel-cycle stages, compressing months of social-engineering groundwork into hours of API interaction. These are adversarial techniques exploiting both the AI system's design (queryable knowledge base with weak input validation) and implicit access-governance failures.

Training-Data Poisoning and Supply-Chain Risk

The continual pre-training pipeline is a high-stealth attack surface: an insider or supply-chain attacker who injects subtly altered technical reports—incorrect safety limits, rearranged procedure steps, or fabricated material-handling guidance—can embed false knowledge into the model's weights that persists across retraining cycles and query sessions. Because the base model (AtomicGPT) and pre-training infrastructure are external artifacts whose provenance KAERI cannot fully verify, a backdoored foundation model or compromised training library could exfiltrate queries, responses, or gradient updates during inference or retraining. The rolling ingestion of internal reports means poisoned documents fold into production with minimal scrutiny (conference-stage evidence suggests no formal data sanitization or red-teaming), and the lack of versioning or source-traceability makes it nearly impossible to identify which report introduced a corrupted procedure. An adversary can time attacks to coincide with known retraining windows, exploiting temporary out-of-distribution behavior or inserting backdoor triggers that only activate after the next training cycle. This is an adversarial manipulation of the AI supply chain (data and software) combined with implicit governance gaps that leave the pipeline undefended.

Hallucination, Cross-Domain Misattribution, and Automation Bias

The model is prone to generating plausible but fabricated technical content—inventing procedural steps, conflating parameters from incompatible facility types (e.g., applying an enrichment criticality limit to a reprocessing scenario), or citing real document numbers with invented summaries—because the ~4,000-report corpus is too small and heterogeneous for robust generalization and the LLM architecture has no ground-truth enforcement. Operators querying the system for institutional knowledge will receive confident, citation-backed answers that may be wrong, and the lack of explainability (no transparent reasoning path from query to source documents) makes it difficult to verify correctness before acting. Automation bias is high: engineers trust the output because it looks authoritative and saves time compared to manual document search, so they stop cross-checking primary sources, and a single hallucinated safety limit or omitted precaution can propagate into operational decisions. This is a purely implicit AI failure (hallucination, opacity, small-data generalization gaps), but it directly enables adversarial exploitation—an attacker who knows the model hallucinates under certain conditions can craft queries to induce operationally dangerous misinformation, or can poison training data knowing that hallucinations will obscure the provenance of false procedures.

Data and Concept Drift with Weak Monitoring

Continual pre-training on a rolling corpus of new reports causes the model's knowledge to drift as older procedures are overwritten or conflated with newer ones, and the on-premise deployment constraint (no cloud MLOps tooling) makes continuous drift detection and retraining-cycle audits unlikely. As facility procedures evolve—new equipment, updated safety analyses, revised material accountancy protocols—the model's answers quietly diverge from current practice, but operators do not notice until a contradiction surfaces in a safety-critical context. Concept drift is especially insidious across the multi-domain corpus: the meaning of a term like 'criticality margin' shifts between enrichment, fuel fabrication, and reprocessing, and the model may apply an outdated or wrong-context definition in its summaries. The static qualification of a conference-stage prototype cannot keep pace with the dynamic operational reality of four facility types, and there is no evidence of versioning, A/B testing, or rollback mechanisms. An adversary who understands the model is outdated (e.g., via public conference presentations or insider knowledge of retraining schedules) can time attacks to exploit stale procedures the model still recommends, or can flood the training pipeline with benign-looking reports that accelerate drift in a target direction. This is implicit drift exacerbating both adversarial and non-adversarial risk.

Need-to-Know Erosion and Access-Governance Failure

The system fundamentally subverts compartmentalization: a user with model access can query technical details from any of the four facility domains in the training corpus, regardless of their role-based need-to-know, because the model has no facility-type or sensitivity-level filters. The 4,000-report corpus almost certainly includes safeguards-sensitive material accountancy data, export-controlled enrichment parameters, and proprietary reprocessing chemistry, all now accessible via natural-language query to anyone on the internal network. There is no mention of query logging, anomaly detection, or role-based output restrictions, so an insider's reconnaissance (e.g., systematically extracting all centrifuge-related summaries) goes unnoticed until exfiltration is complete. The on-premise deployment was intended to satisfy security policy (no cloud data exposure), but it paradoxically creates a weaker access-control perimeter than formal document repositories, because the model is likely deployed on general IT infrastructure with less rigorous segmentation than OT or classified systems. This is an implicit data-governance and security-model failure that adversaries exploit via legitimate but malicious use, and it persists because the conference-stage prototype has no regulatory oversight or AI-specific qualification against insider-threat scenarios.

Cross-Site Propagation and Fleet-Wide Misinformation Risk

Because the model ingests reports from enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and power generation, a single training-data error, hallucination, or poisoned input can propagate misinformation across all four domains if the system is deployed fleet-wide or shared across KAERI facilities. The institutional knowledge-base role means the model becomes a de facto standard reference, and if other sites adopt it (or if a centralized deployment serves multiple facilities), a compromised model corrupts operational practice at scale. The lack of facility-specific output validation or domain-boundary enforcement means a user at an enrichment plant can receive (and act on) a summary derived from reprocessing data, and vice versa, with no mechanism to flag cross-domain contamination. This is implicit cross-site model propagation combined with adversarial supply-chain risk—if an attacker poisons the shared training corpus or backdoors the base model, the attack surface is every facility that queries the system.

Governance Immaturity and Qualification Gaps

This is conference-stage research with no evidence of security review, red-teaming, formal V&V, or alignment with nuclear regulatory frameworks for safety-critical AI. The system was built to solve a convenience problem (cloud LLMs banned by policy), not designed against adversarial threat models, so it almost certainly lacks basic controls like prompt filtering, output sanitization, query-rate limiting, or role-based access restrictions. The on-premise constraint that drove the project paradoxically creates an AI-specific qualification gap: KAERI likely lacks the MLOps infrastructure, adversarial robustness testing, and continuous-monitoring resources that cloud providers bring, and the security-policy compliance (no external data) crowds out investment in internal AI security. There is no mention of software-engineering hygiene (version control for training data, reproducible retraining pipelines, drift dashboards), and the regulatory readiness gap means the system exists in a compliance vacuum—no regulator has evaluated whether an LLM trained on multi-facility technical reports meets safety, security, or safeguards standards. These implicit governance and qualification failures lower the bar for adversarial success (attackers face fewer defenses) and increase the likelihood of non-adversarial catastrophic failures (no process to detect and remediate hallucinations, drift, or misattributions before they cause harm).

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer evaluating operations and safety, my primary concern is that this system ingests thousands of internal technical documents -- operational procedures, maintenance records, equipment specifications, potentially safeguards-sensitive material accountancy reports or facility design details -- and then generates summaries or answers queries about them. The AI becomes a single point where institutional knowledge converges, and if its output drifts, hallucinates, or is manipulated (by poisoned input documents or prompt injection if user queries are allowed), operators or engineers may act on incorrect technical guidance. Because the system is trained on proprietary reports spanning multiple facility types (power, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication), a content error could propagate across very different safety or safeguards contexts -- a fuel-fabrication procedure misattributed to a reprocessing step, or a criticality limit from one domain applied to another. The on-premise deployment mitigates some exfiltration risk, but the lack of cloud-service oversight may also mean weaker MLOps rigor and less transparency into model behavior changes over successive continual pre-training cycles.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Implicit (non-adversarial) vulnerabilities:** The system is prone to hallucination or misattribution of technical content (OP.C0304.01), especially given the diversity of facility domains in its training corpus -- it may confidently generate plausible-sounding but incorrect procedures or technical limits by blending details from incompatible contexts. Continual pre-training on internal reports introduces significant data-drift and concept-drift risk (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02): as new reports accumulate, older knowledge may be overwritten or conflated, and there is no evidence of versioning or drift detection. The system also suffers from explainability limits (OP.C0401) -- if an engineer queries it for a critical parameter and receives a hallucinated value, there is no clear way to trace the answer back to source documents or verify correctness, encouraging automation over-trust (OP.C0101.04). The on-premise deployment, while reducing cloud dependency (OP.C0601), likely exacerbates software-engineering hygiene gaps (OP.C0502) and AI-specific qualification gaps (OP.C0501), since KAERI may lack the MLOps infrastructure and red-teaming resources that cloud providers bring. Finally, because the model spans multiple facility types, there is cross-site propagation risk (OP.C0602): if the model is deployed across KAERI's facilities, a single training-data error or model corruption propagates fleet-wide.

**Adversarial vulnerabilities:** An insider (or supply-chain attacker who compromises the document ingestion pipeline) could poison the training corpus by injecting subtly altered technical reports with incorrect safety limits, procedure steps, or material-handling guidance (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0010.002 AI Supply Chain Compromise - Data). Because the system is continually pre-trained, poisoned documents would be folded into the model's weights and could persist across many query sessions. If the system allows user queries (likely, given its summarization mission), it is vulnerable to prompt injection (AML.T0051.000 Direct, AML.T0051.001 Indirect if it processes user-supplied documents) that could trick it into leaking safeguards-sensitive details from its training data (AML.T0056 Extract LLM System Prompt, AML.T0057 LLM Data Leakage, AML.T0024.000 Infer Training Data Membership) -- for example, an adversary could craft queries to extract enrichment cascade configurations or reprocessing material balances. The system also opens an exfiltration vector: even on-premise, if an adversary gains query access (AML.T0012 Valid Accounts, AML.T0049 Exploit Public-Facing Application if there is a web interface), they can iteratively probe the model to reconstruct proprietary technical knowledge or facility layouts without ever touching the original document store (AML.T0040 AI Model Inference API Access). Finally, the lack of transparency into continual pre-training cycles means an adversary could time an attack to coincide with a known model-update window, exploiting temporary out-of-distribution behavior (OP.C0302 drift exacerbating AML.T0043 Craft Adversarial Data) or inject a backdoor trigger into a document batch that only activates after re-training (AML.T0043.004 Insert Backdoor Trigger).

ai_engineer.argument: This use case lands squarely in my wheelhouse: a domain-specific LLM continuously ingesting internal technical documentation and then serving as an institutional query interface. The ML pipeline has three critical exposure surfaces. First, continual pre-training on ~4,000 internal reports creates a direct exfiltration risk—prompt injection or membership inference can leak report contents, and the model becomes a single-point oracle for an adversary who gains query access. Second, the on-premise constraint (no cloud services due to security policy) likely means limited ML-ops maturity: if retraining cycles are infrequent or if drift monitoring is weak, the model's answers will quietly diverge from current procedures or newly discovered failure modes, and operators may not notice until it contradicts critical safety logic. Third, instruction-tuned LLMs have well-documented jailbreak and prompt-injection vulnerabilities—an adversary (or even an innocent user embedding a malicious string in a uploaded document that later enters the training corpus) can manipulate the model to generate plausible-but-wrong summaries of procedures, effectively poisoning the institutional knowledge base at query time.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: **Adversarial threats:** An attacker with API or chat access can extract training data (technical reports across power, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel-fab) via membership inference (AML.T0024.000) or inversion attacks (AML.T0024.001), circumventing document-access controls. Prompt injection (AML.T0051.000 direct, .001 indirect if the model ever ingests user-supplied text) lets an adversary override system instructions to leak restricted content, generate misleading procedural summaries, or embed false citations that operators trust (AML.T0067.000). If the model is retrained on a rolling window of reports, an insider or supply-chain compromise can poison the training corpus (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) with subtly incorrect procedures that survive into production, effectively a slow-motion data-poisoning campaign with high stealth. Because the system is on-premise and bespoke, adversaries can also use public pre-training of AtomicGPT as a proxy (AML.T0005.002) to craft transferable attacks offline, then deploy them when they gain access. **Implicit (non-adversarial) fragilities that adversaries can exploit or that fail on their own:** The ~4,000-report corpus is almost certainly too small and too homogeneous for robust generalization—model will hallucinate plausible-sounding but fabricated procedures when asked about edge cases or newer operational scenarios not covered in training data (OP.C0304.01 hallucination, OP.C0302.01 data drift, OP.C0202 small-data problem). On-premise deployment with limited MLOps infrastructure makes continuous monitoring and retraining unlikely (OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch, OP.C0502 software-engineering hygiene gaps), so concept drift accumulates silently as facility procedures evolve—operators trust stale summaries, and the adversary who knows the model is outdated can time an attack to exploit that gap (OP.C0302.02 concept drift). Because LLMs are non-deterministic and opaque (OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability, OP.C0401 explainability limit), two users querying the same procedure may get different answers, and there's no audit trail to verify correctness—automation bias (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) is high because the output looks authoritative and cites real documents even when wrong (OP.C0304.02 mistranslation if the model rephrases critical steps). The institutional knowledge-base role means a single compromised model propagates misinformation fleet-wide if other sites adopt it (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), and the security-policy constraint that drove on-premise deployment paradoxically creates a qualification gap (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap) because the team likely lacks resources to do adversarial robustness testing or formal V&V at the pace needed for a continuously retrained LLM.

security_specialist.argument: This use case sits at a dangerous intersection: it concentrates institutional knowledge (4,000 internal technical reports spanning fuel cycle facilities) into a single queryable artifact, accessible on-premises to anyone with network credentials, and the model's training corpus becomes a persistent insider-threat target rather than ephemeral human memory. A sophisticated adversary—especially a nation-state with pre-positioned insiders or supply-chain access—would find this model an extraordinarily high-value stepping stone: compromise it once (via prompt extraction, model exfiltration, or simply legitimate but malicious use), and you gain a curated map of an entire institution's technical practices, vulnerabilities, and operational details across enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and power generation. Even non-adversarial failure modes (hallucination, over-summarization, misattribution of sensitive details) erode the 'need-to-know' boundaries that security culture depends on, because users will query across facility types they wouldn't normally access, and the model won't enforce compartmentalization. The system also creates a new category of high-privilege account (model access = access to cross-facility knowledge), which is exactly what an insider-threat or compromised-credential scenario exploits, and the on-premise deployment constraint means security monitoring is likely ad-hoc rather than cloud-vendor-grade.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) The model itself is a concentration-of-knowledge target: exfiltrating the fine-tuned weights or training corpus yields a pre-digested intelligence product spanning multiple facility types, far more valuable than piecemeal document theft (AML.T0024.002 Extract AI Model, AML.T0048.004 AI Intellectual Property Theft). An insider with legitimate model access can extract operational details from facilities they'd never visit (e.g., an enrichment-site worker querying reprocessing practices), bypassing physical and role-based access controls. (2) Prompt injection or jailbreak (AML.T0051, AML.T0054) could compel the model to leak compartmented information, and the lack of robust input validation in a research/conference-stage system makes this trivially executable. (3) The on-premise constraint likely means the model runs on general IT infrastructure with weaker physical/cyber segmentation than OT systems, so a network-level compromise (AML.T0049 Exploit Public-Facing Application, AML.T0012 Valid Accounts) offers a stepping stone to the model, and from there to actionable intelligence about critical facilities. (4) Supply-chain risk (AML.T0010.003 Model, AML.T0010.001 AI Software): the base model (AtomicGPT) and continual pre-training pipeline are external artifacts whose provenance KAERI cannot fully verify, and a backdoored base model could exfiltrate queries or responses during inference. (5) The model changes the threat calculus for social engineering: an adversary can use it (via a compromised or coerced insider) to rapidly prototype plausible technical scenarios for further attacks, since it 'understands' institutional norms and jargon across fuel-cycle domains.

IMPLICIT/NON-ADVERSARIAL THREATS THAT ADVERSARIES EXPLOIT: (1) Hallucination/misattribution (OP.C0304.01) is catastrophic here—if the model invents a procedural detail or conflates facilities, operators may act on false information, and an adversary timing an attack can exploit the resulting confusion or procedural misstep. (2) The model erodes 'need-to-know' discipline (OP.C0505 Data access governance, OP.C0505.01 Inappropriate data security model): users will query it for convenience rather than formal document requests, and there's no evidence of query logging or anomaly detection, so an insider's reconnaissance (e.g., 'summarize all reports mentioning [safeguards equipment]') goes unnoticed. (3) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04 Misuse/over-trust): if the model becomes the first-line reference for institutional knowledge, engineers stop cross-checking primary sources, and an adversary who has poisoned the training corpus (or exploited drift) can propagate false information that operators trust. (4) Data provenance opacity (OP.C0201): 4,000 reports is a large, unstructured corpus—there's no indication KAERI sanitized or compartmented it before training, so the model may encode near-export-controlled details (e.g., centrifuge cascade parameters, reprocessing chemistry) that a determined adversary could extract via membership inference (AML.T0024.000). (5) Governance immaturity (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0504 Regulatory readiness gap): this is conference-stage research with no mention of security review, red-teaming, or alignment with nuclear regulatory frameworks—it was built to solve a convenience problem (can't use cloud LLMs), not designed against adversarial threat models, so it's almost certainly missing basic controls like prompt filtering, output sanitization, or role-based query restrictions. (6) The model is a persistent, queryable artifact that doesn't forget or retire: unlike a human expert who leaves or dies, this knowledge base remains accessible indefinitely, and over time it accumulates institutional drift (OP.C0302.01) and becomes a 'time capsule' an adversary can exploit years later when security postures have changed but the model hasn't been retrained.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on prompt injection / data leakage, training-data poisoning, hallucination / misattribution, drift (data and concept), automation bias, and governance / qualification gaps as the core threats; the security specialist's need-to-know erosion and the AI engineer's small-data problem were retained as distinct but complementary to the shared cross-domain misattribution concern.

evidence.citation: Yeom, S. & Yu, Y. (KAERI) (2026), "KAERI-GPT: Extending a Nuclear Domain LLM to Secure Institutional Environments," Transactions of the Korean Nuclear Society Spring Meeting (conference paper)
evidence.note: Extends AtomicGPT with about 4,000 internal technical reports via on-premise continual pre-training and instruction tuning, since cloud LLM services are barred by security policy. Conference-level evidence only.

damage.why: Adversarial exfiltration of safeguards-sensitive information (cascade configurations, material accountancy procedures) or propagation of poisoned procedures across enrichment/reprocessing facilities directly enables safeguards falsification and loss of material control.

reproducibility.why: Prompt injection to extract cross-domain technical details and hallucination-driven misinformation are reliably triggered by crafted queries or routine use, though training-data poisoning requires precise timing with retraining cycles.

exploitability.why: Adversarial exfiltration and reconnaissance require only legitimate or compromised credentials for query access (routine internal interaction), while training-data poisoning requires insider access to the document ingestion pipeline but no nation-state tooling.

affected_users.why: The system serves all four facility domains (enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, power generation) and a single poisoned input or hallucinated procedure can propagate misinformation fleet-wide across coupled fuel-cycle operations.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class is inferable from the publicly documented conference paper describing on-premise LLM deployment with continual pre-training on multi-facility reports, making query-based exfiltration and lack of access controls evident to capable outsiders familiar with LLM attack literature.

use_case: Predicting (using, e.g., temporal convolutional network) remaining useful life of electric gate valves in nuclear power plant control systems for predictive maintenance
incurred_insecurity:
Deploying an AI model to predict remaining useful life of safety-critical electric gate valves in reactor control systems introduces both implicit operational vulnerabilities and adversarial attack surfaces that compound into a systemic risk. The model's predictions directly govern maintenance schedules and operator vigilance for components whose failure can compromise reactor cooling, reactivity control, or containment isolation. When the model is trained on experimental bench data rather than decades of in-situ operational history, it may miss plant-specific degradation modes—radiation effects, thermal cycling unique to reactor transients, or lubricant chemistry changes—leading to concept drift and out-of-distribution failures that manifest as undetected valve degradation. Simultaneously, an adversary who compromises the model's training data, input sensor streams, or inference outputs can mask real failures (inducing reliance on false assurances of valve health) or fabricate alarms (creating maintenance fatigue and access opportunities), timing these manipulations to coincide with safety-critical events or exploiting the model's opacity to evade detection.

Data Provenance and the Small-Data Problem
The model learns from experimental accelerated-life testing (bench-measured data) rather than long-term operational field data, creating a fundamental mismatch between the training environment and the reactor control-system service conditions the valves will experience. This is an implicit data-provenance weakness: the experimental dataset cannot capture the full spectrum of aging mechanisms—radiation embrittlement of actuator components, micro-debris ingress in high-radiation zones, or the interaction of thermal cycling with specific valve service histories—unique to each plant's multi-decade operational envelope. Compounding this, catastrophic valve failures are rare by design, so the training set systematically undersamples the critical transition from degraded-but-functional to failed, forcing the temporal convolutional network to extrapolate in precisely the regime where prediction errors have the highest safety consequence. An adversary aware of these training-data gaps—potentially via exfiltration of the model or its training metadata—can induce the under-represented failure modes covertly (for example, through cyber-physical manipulation of actuator power supplies or subtle alteration of valve operating profiles) confident that the model will not flag the degradation. This is an implicit vulnerability (small-data and data-provenance mismatch) that becomes an exploitable adversarial entry point.

Concept Drift and Operational Heterogeneity
As the plant ages, undergoes power uprates, or modifies operating procedures, valve degradation signatures shift—cycles-to-failure curves steepen, thermal stress patterns change, or new actuator designs with different wear characteristics are introduced—yet the static model retains its original training-era assumptions. This concept drift occurs without adversarial action but degrades the model's predictive accuracy over time, widening the gap between predicted and actual remaining useful life. An adversary can accelerate this drift covertly by subtly altering valve operating conditions via compromised control logic (for example, increasing actuation frequency or changing the valve's duty cycle in ways that mimic normal operations but accelerate wear), then exploit the widening blind spot: the model confidently predicts long remaining life while the valve approaches failure under the novel stress regime. Operational heterogeneity across a multi-unit fleet exacerbates this—valves in different units experience different radiation fields, coolant chemistries, and maintenance histories, yet a single fleet-wide model may be deployed without plant-specific retraining, creating systematic under-prediction or over-prediction at specific sites that an adversary can target selectively.

Training-Data Poisoning for Timed Safety-System Unavailability
If an adversary gains write access to the historical maintenance logs, sensor baselines, or data historian feeding the model's training pipeline—either through a long-term insider position or compromise of the engineering workstation network—they can inject subtly manipulated records that bias the model's learned degradation signature. For example, falsifying historical failure events to appear later in a valve's service life than they actually occurred, or suppressing anomaly flags in the training data, causes the model to systematically under-predict remaining useful life for targeted valve types or operating regimes. The result is deferred maintenance on valves the adversary knows are nearing failure, creating a window of reduced safety-system redundancy that can be timed to coincide with other attack steps (such as a cyber intrusion targeting reactor control during a planned maintenance outage when the poisoned model has convinced operators to leave a degraded valve in service). Conversely, systematic over-prediction through poisoned training data drives unnecessary maintenance, creating alert fatigue, eroding operator trust in the model, and generating frequent access opportunities for insider actions during the resulting maintenance windows. This adversarial threat is a direct manipulation of the AI training process.

Inference-Time Adversarial Manipulation and Model Evasion
An adversary with access to the sensor streams feeding the model—vibration monitors, motor current signatures, position encoders, or temperature sensors on the valve actuators—can craft adversarial time-series inputs designed to suppress the model's failure warnings. Using black-box optimization against a proxy model (which the adversary may have trained by exfiltrating the plant's model or by observing input-output pairs via the inference API), the attacker identifies subtle perturbations to the sensor traces that cause the temporal convolutional network to output a benign remaining-useful-life estimate even as the valve is being covertly degraded through physical or cyber means. This evasion tactic masks sabotage in real time: the model continues to report the valve as healthy, maintenance is deferred, and the degradation becomes visible only when the valve fails to actuate during a safety-critical transient. The adversary's manipulation can be persistent if they maintain access to the sensor network, or it can be a one-time injection timed to a high-consequence scenario (for example, during reactor startup or a design-basis event when the valve's function is demanded). This is a classic adversarial AI attack applied to a safety-critical cyber-physical control loop.

Automation Bias, Alarm Complacency, and Exploited Trust Dynamics
When operators and maintenance planners come to rely on the model's predictions, they reduce traditional condition-monitoring practices—periodic manual stroke testing, trending of diagnostic parameters, or walk-down inspections—and trust the AI-generated schedule as ground truth. This automation-induced complacency is an implicit human-factors vulnerability: a miscalibrated model or one subjected to adversarial manipulation will not be cross-checked, so its errors propagate directly into operational decisions. An adversary exploits this by timing attacks to periods when the model predicts long remaining useful life and operator vigilance is lowest, or by first inducing a series of false alarms (via data manipulation causing over-prediction) to create alert fatigue, then introducing a real fault that operators dismiss as another false positive. The model's opacity exacerbates this dynamic—because the temporal convolutional network's internal reasoning is not transparent, operators cannot audit whether a prediction is driven by genuine physical degradation signatures or by adversarial noise, and there is no procedural requirement to verify AI outputs against independent condition indicators before altering surveillance schedules.

Model Exfiltration, Offline Analysis, and Blind-Spot Discovery
A sophisticated adversary, particularly a nation-state actor with long-term strategic interest in the facility, can exfiltrate the trained model or reconstruct it via systematic querying of the inference API, then analyze it offline to map its failure-mode coverage and identify which degradation mechanisms it systematically misses. This intelligence-gathering step informs subsequent sabotage: the adversary knows which failure signatures are out-of-distribution for the model and can induce those specific failure modes (via cyber-physical manipulation or insider action) confident that the AI monitoring system will not detect them. The exfiltration itself is an adversarial technique, and the resulting knowledge asymmetry—where the adversary understands the model's blind spots better than the defenders—transforms the predictive maintenance system into a strategic liability.

Supply-Chain Compromise of Training Data or Model Artifacts
If the experimental dataset, pre-trained model weights, or data-preprocessing code are sourced from external collaborators, vendors, or open repositories, an adversary can poison them at the source before they ever reach the plant. This supply-chain attack embeds backdoors or biases into the model's learned parameters, which activate under specific plant conditions (for example, a particular combination of temperature and actuation frequency) or at a predetermined time. The plant's qualification process, if it lacks adversarial robustness testing or provenance auditing, may not detect the compromise, and the poisoned model is deployed across the fleet. The adversary then waits for the trigger condition or timeline, at which point the model's predictions become unreliable in a coordinated, multi-site fashion, enabling simultaneous attacks on safety-system availability across the fleet.

Cross-Site Model Propagation and Fleet-Wide Risk Amplification
If the same model or training dataset is deployed across multiple reactor units or plants—a common practice in fleet-wide predictive maintenance programs to reduce per-unit qualification costs—a single poisoning event, miscalibration, or adversarial compromise propagates the vulnerability across the entire fleet. This architectural decision amplifies the adversary's return on investment: one successful supply-chain attack, one insider campaign at a central engineering office, or one undetected drift event affects dozens of safety-critical valves across multiple sites simultaneously. An adversary can exploit this by targeting the central model repository or the shared data infrastructure, creating coordinated vulnerabilities that manifest as simultaneous valve failures or undetected degradation at multiple plants, overwhelming the utility's incident-response capacity and creating strategic instability.

Qualification, Governance, and the Static-Dynamic Mismatch
The model was qualified using an experimental dataset under a static set of assumptions, but its operational deployment subjects it to a continuously evolving context—procedure changes, vendor variability in replacement valve components, shifts in plant operating profiles, and long-term aging effects. There is no AI-specific regulatory standard or qualification framework that mandates continuous revalidation, adversarial robustness testing, drift monitoring, or explainability audits for safety-critical RUL predictions in nuclear facilities. This governance gap means the model may drift out of its qualified envelope without triggering any formal re-assessment, and adversaries aware of this can time their attacks to coincide with periods when the qualification is most stale. The lack of transparency (temporal convolutional networks are opaque, offering no feature-importance maps or residual analysis in operational use) further limits the plant's ability to detect when the model has diverged from physical reality, whether through natural drift or adversarial manipulation.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations lens, this use case introduces significant risk through automation complacency and hidden single points of failure. If the AI model incorrectly predicts longer remaining useful life than actual (a false-negative on degradation), operators may defer maintenance on a safety-critical valve until it fails in service—potentially during a transient when that valve's function is demanded. Conversely, overly conservative predictions (false-positives) that trigger unnecessary maintenance create new human-performance challenges (rework fatigue, opportunity for maintenance-induced faults) and erode trust, leading to eventual disuse of the system. The reliance on experimental bench data rather than years of in-situ operational history means the model may not capture real degradation modes (thermal cycling, radiation effects on actuator components, lubrication chemistry changes) unique to each plant's environment. Because this is valve-level predictive maintenance—not a system-level integrity model—there is no inherent cross-check: a single miscalibrated model could propagate across an entire fleet if deployed centrally, and operators have no procedural requirement to verify AI output against independent condition indicators (stroke time, motor current signature) before altering surveillance schedules.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The primary operational threat is **automation-induced complacency leading to a missed degradation event** (OP.C0101.04 misuse / OP.C0102 alarm complacency). Operators and maintenance planners, seeing consistent AI-generated RUL estimates, may reduce or eliminate traditional condition-monitoring practices (periodic stroke testing, trending of diagnostic parameters) and rely solely on the AI schedule. If the model's training data came from laboratory accelerated-life testing and does not reflect plant-specific stressors—radiation, temperature transients, or unique valve service conditions—this is a **data-provenance and drift failure** (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). A valve that the model rates as healthy may fail unexpectedly during a safety actuation (e.g., emergency feedwater isolation, containment isolation), and because there is no independent confirmation loop, **the system creates a hidden single point of failure**. 

From an adversarial perspective, an attacker who compromises the AI model or its input data stream (sensor spoofing, training data injection if the model is retrained online) can **deliberately mask valve degradation** to engineer a failure on demand (AML.T0018.000 poison AI model, AML.T0020 poison training data, AML.T0015 evade AI model). For example, subtly altering vibration or current signatures fed to the TCN during inference could suppress warnings on a targeted valve; the adversary then waits for a scenario where that valve's failure has maximum consequence (e.g., during a design-basis accident when the valve must reposition). This is exacerbated by **fleet-wide model propagation** (OP.C0602): a single backdoored or miscalibrated model deployed across multiple units means one compromise scales across the fleet. Because RUL prediction lacks explainability (OP.C0401), operators cannot easily detect when the model's internal reasoning has diverged from physical reality—there is no transparent feature importance or residual analysis in operational use. Additionally, **concept drift** (OP.C0302.02) is a non-adversarial but exploitable risk: as valve designs are updated, lubricants changed, or environmental conditions shift (e.g., post-uprate thermal conditions), the model's learned degradation signatures become stale, but no automatic requalification trigger exists (OP.C0303 static/dynamic mismatch, OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap). An adversary aware of this drift window can time an attack to coincide with periods when the model is least reliable.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case trains a temporal convolutional network on experimental valve-degradation data to predict remaining useful life for reactor control-system gate valves. From an ML-engineering perspective, the central fragility is representativeness: the TCN learns from a lab or test-stand dataset that may not capture the full operational envelope (temperature cycling, radiation exposure, valve cycling under varying system transients) that real control-system valves experience over decades. At inference, the model encounters sensor traces from fielded valves whose degradation modes may differ from what the experimental dataset encoded—classic out-of-distribution drift. Additionally, because catastrophic valve failures are rare by design (low base rate), the training set likely undersamples failure-proximate regimes, so the TCN's predictions in the critical tail of the RUL distribution are poorly calibrated. If plant staff trust these predictions to defer inspections or skip scheduled replacements, a misclassified valve (predicted safe, actually near failure) in a reactor control loop creates both a safety exposure (loss of control actuation when needed) and a security one (an adversary timing an attack to coincide with undetected valve degradation, or poisoning the sensor stream to mask incipient failure and induce reliance on the faulty prediction).
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary ML-pipeline vulnerabilities are data-provenance mismatch (OP.C0201.04: the experimental dataset is bench-measured, not field/operational, so it may omit aging mechanisms unique to in-service reactor environments—radiation embrittlement, thermal cycling specific to control-rod actuation sequences, or micro-debris ingress in high-radiation zones) and the low-base-rate problem (OP.C0202: actual valve failures are rare, so the training set has few or no examples of the transition from degraded-but-functional to failed, forcing the TCN to extrapolate). These non-adversarial gaps create adversarial attack surfaces: an adversary with write access to the sensor feeds (vibration, current draw, position encoder) could craft adversarial time-series inputs (AML.T0043.001: black-box optimization against a proxy TCN) that suppress the RUL alarm, causing maintenance deferral on a valve the adversary knows is degrading. Alternatively, data/concept drift (OP.C0302.01/02) occurs naturally as valve operating profiles shift (e.g., post-uprate the valves cycle more frequently, or a design change alters the actuator torque curve), invalidating the TCN's learned degradation signature without retraining—no adversary needed, but this undetected drift similarly results in missed failures. If the plant deploys this TCN across multiple units (OP.C0602: cross-site model propagation), a single poisoned training batch or a miscalibrated model propagates fleet-wide, amplifying the safety and security consequences. The governance gap (OP.C0501: no AI-specific qualification standard for safety-critical RUL predictions in nuclear) means there may be no required adversarial-robustness testing or drift-monitoring regime, leaving these ML failure modes unaudited until a valve fails unexpectedly. Finally, because the TCN is opaque (OP.C0401: explainability limit), operators cannot easily distinguish a genuine near-end-of-life signature from adversarially injected noise or drift-induced misclassification, so automation-trust failures (OP.C0101.04: misuse/over-trust) compound the risk—staff may skip manual inspections based on a confident but wrong RUL estimate, and the resulting undetected valve failure in a control loop degrades both reactor-protection response (safety) and creates an exploitable window for adversaries targeting reactor control availability or manipulating safety-system state.

security_specialist.argument: Electric gate valves in reactor control systems are safety-critical components whose availability and state directly affect core cooling, reactivity control, and containment isolation — their failure or unexpected unavailability can trigger scram or loss of safety function. Introducing an AI-driven predictive maintenance model creates a high-value insider target: an adversary with access to the model's inputs (sensor streams, operational telemetry) or outputs (maintenance schedules, predicted failure windows) gains intelligence on when safety systems will be degraded or offline, enabling timed attacks during maintenance windows or false-alarm fatigue campaigns. The model also consolidates trust: if operators come to rely on its RUL estimates, an adversary who can poison its training data (e.g., by subtly manipulating historical failure records or sensor baselines during an extended insider campaign) can cause it to under-predict failures (leading to unplanned outages or safety system unavailability at a chosen time) or over-predict them (driving unnecessary maintenance that creates access opportunities or fatigues staff). Even without direct adversarial action, the model's non-adversarial failure modes — concept drift as valve degradation mechanisms change with plant aging, small-data problems if the training set lacks certain failure modes, and opacity that makes it hard to verify the model isn't systematically biased — are themselves what an adversary would exploit: a nation-state attacker would study the model's training dataset (possibly exfiltrated or inferred via side channels) to understand which failure signatures it misses, then induce those signatures covertly (e.g., via cyber-physical manipulation of valve actuators or power supplies) to create failures the model won't predict, undermining defense-in-depth when it matters most.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) Intelligence value — the model's input features (sensor telemetry, actuation logs, thermal/vibration signatures) and output (predicted failure date/probability) collectively map the real-time health and near-term availability of safety-critical valves; an insider or remote attacker gaining read access to model I/O learns when valves will be taken offline for maintenance (creating windows of reduced redundancy) or when the plant expects a valve to remain healthy (enabling surprise sabotage). This is a persistent surveillance capability if the adversary can access the model's inference API or the data historian feeding it. (2) Training-data poisoning for timed unavailability — if an adversary can inject false or manipulated historical records (e.g., via compromised maintenance logs, historian tampering, or a long-term insider campaign), they can bias the model to under-predict RUL for specific valve types or operating regimes, causing the plant to defer maintenance until a failure occurs during a critical transient (e.g., reactor startup, power maneuver, or accident scenario requiring isolation). Alternatively, systematic over-prediction drives unnecessary maintenance, creating access opportunities for further insider actions and fatiguing operators who see frequent false alarms. (3) Inference-time adversarial manipulation — if the adversary has cyber access to the sensor streams or data preprocessing pipeline, they can craft inputs (e.g., subtly altered vibration spectra, temperature trends, or actuation-cycle counts) that cause the model to output a benign RUL estimate even as the valve is being covertly degraded; this is a 'cover' for sabotage, making the degradation invisible to automated monitoring until it manifests as a failure. (4) Model exfiltration and offline analysis (ATLAS T0024.002) — a sophisticated attacker (especially nation-state) could exfiltrate the trained model or reconstruct it via black-box querying, then use offline analysis to discover which failure modes it systematically misses or which input perturbations fool it; this intelligence informs physical or cyber sabotage campaigns targeting the model's blind spots. (5) Supply-chain risk in model or training data (ATLAS T0010.002, T0010.003) — if the experimental dataset or pre-trained TCN weights are sourced from external collaborators or vendors, an adversary could have poisoned them at the source, embedding backdoors that activate under specific plant conditions or timeframes.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) VULNERABILITIES THAT ADVERSARIES EXPLOIT OR TIME ATTACKS AROUND: (1) Small-data / low base-rate problem (OP.C0202) — the experimental dataset likely captures only a subset of valve failure modes (e.g., electrical faults, mechanical binding, actuator motor degradation, seal leakage); rare or novel failure mechanisms (which an adversary might induce covertly) may be out-of-distribution, causing the model to confidently predict long RUL even as the valve approaches failure. An attacker aware of this gap can induce the under-represented failure mode and rely on the model's blind spot to delay detection. (2) Concept drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03) — valve degradation rates and signatures change with plant aging, power uprates, changes in operating procedures, or environmental conditions (e.g., increased radiation exposure, temperature cycling); if the model is not continuously retrained with field data from the specific plant and valve population, it will drift. An adversary can accelerate drift covertly (e.g., by subtly altering valve operating conditions over time via compromised control logic) and exploit the widening gap between model predictions and reality. The paper's reliance on experimental (lab) data rather than full operational data exacerbates this — the model may not capture the multi-unit, multi-cycle wear patterns of real reactor service. (3) Automation bias and alarm complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102) — if operators come to trust the model's RUL predictions, they may reduce manual inspections, overlook early physical symptoms (unusual noise, slower actuation), or dismiss anomalies flagged by other systems ('the AI says the valve is fine'). An adversary times their attack to exploit this complacency: they act during a period when the model predicts high RUL and operators are least vigilant. If the model has previously issued false alarms (over-prediction leading to unnecessary maintenance), operators may also experience alert fatigue and ignore warnings when a real failure is imminent — a scenario an insider could engineer by first poisoning data to cause over-prediction, then inducing a real fault. (4) Explainability and opacity (OP.C0401) — TCNs are difficult to interpret; operators and engineers cannot easily verify *why* the model predicts a specific RUL or audit whether its reasoning is sound. This limits the ability to spot adversarial manipulation or data-quality issues and creates a trust-but-cannot-verify dynamic that an adversary exploits by ensuring their manipulations are subtle enough to evade statistical anomaly detection but effective enough to bias predictions. (5) Qualification and drift mismatch (OP.C0303) — the model was qualified on an experimental dataset, but its real-world deployment subjects it to evolving operational contexts (procedure changes, valve replacements, vendor variability in valve components). An adversary aware that the plant has not continuously re-validated the model can exploit the qualification gap by introducing failure modes or operating conditions the model was never tested against. (6) Cross-site model propagation (OP.C0602) — if the same model or training dataset is deployed across multiple units or plants (common in fleet-wide predictive maintenance), a single poisoning event or model compromise propagates the vulnerability across the fleet, amplifying the adversary's return on investment and enabling coordinated, multi-site attacks.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the data-provenance mismatch (bench vs. operational data), concept drift, automation bias, model opacity, and cross-site propagation as core vulnerabilities; the security specialist's detailed adversarial scenarios (training poisoning, inference evasion, exfiltration, supply-chain) were retained as they represent distinct attack vectors built on the implicit weaknesses the nuclear and AI engineers identified.

evidence.citation: Wang, H., Peng, M., Xu, R., Ayodeji, A. & Xia, H. (2020), "Remaining Useful Life Prediction Based on Improved Temporal Convolutional Network for Nuclear Power Plant Valves," Frontiers in Energy Research 8, 584463
evidence.note: RUL prediction verified on an electric gate valve experimental dataset representing valves in the reactor control system.

damage.why: Undetected degradation or adversarially-masked failure of safety-critical electric gate valves in reactor control systems can directly compromise reactor cooling, reactivity control, or containment isolation, leading to radiological release or loss of safety function during design-basis events.

reproducibility.why: Concept drift from training-data mismatch and operational changes will reliably degrade model accuracy over time without adversarial action; adversarial poisoning or sensor manipulation, once conditions are met (access to training pipeline or sensor streams), can reliably bias predictions given the model's opacity and lack of continuous revalidation.

exploitability.why: Training-data poisoning and inference-time sensor manipulation require insider access to engineering networks, data historians, or control-system sensor streams; supply-chain compromise of experimental datasets or model artifacts requires vendor-level positioning; these are moderately specialized but within reach of capable adversaries with plant or vendor access, not requiring nation-state-exclusive resources.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide model deployment propagates vulnerabilities across multiple reactor units or plants simultaneously, affecting dozens of safety-critical valves in parallel and overwhelming incident-response capacity; within a single facility, compromised RUL predictions impact multiple valve-dependent safety systems (cooling, reactivity control, containment).

discoverability.why: The use of bench-measured experimental data for RUL prediction, temporal convolutional network architecture, and deployment in predictive maintenance for safety-critical valves are documented in the open literature (cited source); a capable adversary with vendor documentation or procurement records can infer that training-data mismatch, drift vulnerabilities, and adversarial manipulation opportunities exist for this class of AI system without needing insider knowledge of a specific plant's implementation details.

use_case: Large-language-model tutor grounded in facility procedures and NRC reactor fundamentals that delivers personalised instruction to research-reactor operator trainees
incurred_insecurity:
This use case incurs insecurity by embedding an AI tutor into the formative training pipeline for research-reactor operators, where errors in instructional content, retrieval fidelity, or trainee trust propagate directly into licensed operator decision-making at the control board. The dominant implicit threats are hallucination and procedural misattribution that teach incorrect emergency responses or conflate procedures across reactor types, automation over-trust that erodes independent judgment and skill in cross-checking source documents, and operational drift as facility procedures and NRC guidance evolve but the model's knowledge base remains static. Adversarially, the system is a high-leverage target: poisoning training data or the RAG retrieval corpus enables an attacker to systematically degrade operator competence across entire cohorts, and prompt injection or data exfiltration can leak facility-specific vulnerabilities or procedural details that inform later physical or cyber attacks.

Content Fidelity Failure and Hallucination
Large language models inherently risk generating plausible but factually incorrect text, and in this domain a hallucinated procedure step, invented regulatory citation, or oversimplified emergency-response heuristic becomes internalized operator knowledge with no downstream interlock to catch the error before it reaches the simulator or control room. Research reactors span diverse designs (TRIGA, pool-type, fast spectrum); if the model's training corpus mixes these without clear boundaries or includes generic power-reactor materials, trainees learn blended half-truths or procedures applicable to the wrong reactor class. This is an implicit failure in the AI system itself that degrades training quality even without an adversary, but creates exploitable knowledge gaps an attacker aware of the model's weaknesses could trigger during a coordinated event.

Automation Over-Trust and Skill Fade
Trainees, especially junior ones, may over-rely on the AI tutor's confident, personalized answers without cross-checking official procedures or simulator feedback, leading to a habit of seeking AI permission rather than applying regulatory limits and defense-in-depth logic independently. Instructors kept "in the loop" may develop monitoring fatigue if the system usually performs well, failing to catch nuanced degradation or to audit every individualized tutoring session. Over time, this erodes the trainee's skill in independent problem-solving and critical evaluation of information sources—a form of cognitive skill fade that leaves operators hesitant, dependent, or prone to mode errors when the AI is unavailable or when real-world conditions deviate from training scenarios. This implicit weakness is a direct consequence of how humans interact with persuasive automation in high-stakes learning contexts.

Operational and Concept Drift
Research-reactor procedures evolve, NRC guidance updates, and facility-specific operating experience feeds back into training material, but if the fine-tuned model or its RAG knowledge base is not continuously retrained and re-qualified, it will teach outdated or superseded procedures. The small-data problem is acute: operational data and incident libraries for research reactors are sparse compared to commercial power, so the model may fill gaps with analogies from other industries or general LLM priors that do not map to nuclear-specific safety logic. An adversary aware of this staleness could time an attack to exploit the knowledge gap, or an insider could delay updates to maximize the window during which operators are trained on obsolete material. This is an implicit drift in the AI system's alignment with ground truth, exacerbated by the lack of ML-specific qualification processes to verify generalization and by the static nature of fine-tuning against a dynamic operational environment.

Training Data and RAG Corpus Poisoning
An adversarial insider or supply-chain attacker with access to the fine-tuning dataset, procedure documents ingested into the RAG system, or the model update pipeline can embed subtle procedural misguidance—swapping interlock setpoints, reversing emergency-procedure steps, teaching that certain alarms are nuisance and may be silenced, or normalizing shortcuts that bypass safety interlocks. Because the system is pedagogical and trainees are still forming mental models, these errors are internalized as correct and propagate across cohorts without triggering traditional IT security alarms. If the LLM or RAG infrastructure is shared across multiple research reactors or updated centrally, a single compromise enables fleet-wide degradation of training quality—a high-leverage, persistent attack that pre-positions human failure for later exploitation during a time-sensitive scenario. This is an adversarial manipulation of the AI system's knowledge base and constitutes a supply-chain compromise targeting data integrity.

Prompt Injection and Instructional Manipulation
If the tutor ingests trainee questions, facility documents, or external retrieval content without robust input sanitization, a malicious trainee or attacker with user-level access could inject prompts that cause the model to teach incorrect scram criteria, disable procedural checks in its explanations, or reveal sensitive procedural details and operator performance gaps. The model's persuasive, authoritative style amplifies impact: trainees are unlikely to cross-check every AI-delivered answer against hard-copy technical specifications, and instructors may not detect manipulation if the outputs remain superficially plausible. Indirect prompt injection via poisoned retrieval content in the RAG database enables persistent, stealthy instructional sabotage that does not require repeated access once the malicious payload is embedded. This is an adversarial technique executed against the AI system to corrupt its outputs during inference.

Data Exfiltration and Operational Intelligence Leakage
Trainees naturally input facility-specific details—outage schedules, which interlocks frequently trip, gaps in their own understanding of security plans, or questions about off-nominal scenarios—during tutoring sessions, and if those interaction logs are accessible to an adversary or if the model's context window leaks via prompt extraction or API abuse, the attacker gains a detailed map of site-specific vulnerabilities, operator knowledge gaps, and procedural weak points. The system necessarily encodes facility procedures, NRC regulatory interpretations, and potentially security-sensitive operational details in its RAG database and fine-tuned weights; an adversary with API access or who compromises the retrieval infrastructure can invert the model or exfiltrate training data membership to reconstruct protected information. Credential harvesting from improperly secured LLM configurations or RAG datastores provides lateral-movement opportunities into broader facility IT or operational technology networks. This is adversarial exfiltration through the AI system's inference API and data repositories.

Explainability and Qualification Gaps
The LLM's reasoning is opaque: instructors cannot easily verify why the model recommended a particular learning path or which source it actually relied on (as opposed to post-hoc citation), and the model's non-determinism means the same trainee question may yield different answers due to sampling variance, undermining auditability and making it difficult to systematically verify alignment with regulatory requirements. There is no established ML-specific qualification framework for this application, so the system may be statically qualified during initial deployment but never re-verified as procedures change or as the model encounters the long tail of trainee questions in production. This implicit limitation in the AI system's verifiability and repeatability is not adversarial in origin but creates gaps that adversaries can exploit and that hinder detection of both adversarial and non-adversarial failures.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations and engineering practice perspective, this use case poses significant risks because it shapes operator mental models and procedural understanding during formative training—errors or gaps here propagate directly into licensed operator decision-making at the board. The AI tutor's persuasiveness and apparent authority could embed misconceptions or oversimplified heuristics that erode procedural rigor, especially if trainees learn to trust LLM outputs over official procedures or simulator feedback. Because research reactors often have smaller, less-standardized training programs than commercial power plants, instructors may lack resources to systematically audit what the AI is teaching each trainee, and trainees may not recognize when the model hallucinates procedure steps or conflates conditions across different reactor types. The physical consequence is not immediate—no single bad answer crashes the reactor—but the cumulative effect is operators who may hesitate, misdiagnose, or bypass interlocks because their foundational training was subtly wrong.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The dominant non-adversarial threat is **content fidelity failure** (OP.C0304): the LLM may hallucinate procedure steps, invent plausible-sounding but incorrect technical explanations, or conflate NRC guidance applicable to one reactor class with this facility's specific procedures (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03). Research reactors span diverse designs (TRIGA, pool-type, fast spectrum), and if the model's training corpus mixes these or includes generic power-reactor materials without clear boundaries, trainees learn blended half-truths. **Automation trust failure** (OP.C0101.04, misuse/over-trust) is acute here: trainees, especially junior ones, may defer to the AI's confident tone over their own emerging judgment or even over written procedures, leading to **skill fade** (OP.C0101.06) in independent problem-solving and a dangerous habit of seeking AI permission rather than applying regulatory limits and procedures directly. **Explainability limits** (OP.C0401) mean instructors cannot easily verify *why* the model recommended a particular learning path or *which source* it drew an answer from, even with cited traceability, because LLM citations can be post-hoc rationalizations rather than the actual reasoning chain. **Small-data problems** (OP.C0202) are severe: research-reactor operational data and incident libraries are sparse compared to commercial power, so the model may fill gaps with aircraft/chemical-plant analogies or general LLM priors that don't map to nuclear-specific defense-in-depth logic. **Operational drift** (OP.C0302.01) will occur as the facility updates procedures or as NRC guidance evolves, but the fine-tuned model remains static unless continuously retrained—trainees then learn outdated practices. 

Adversarially, this system is a **high-value soft target** because it directly influences operator cognition without triggering traditional IT security alarms. An insider or external attacker who compromises the training corpus or fine-tuning data (AML.T0020, Poison Training Data; AML.T0010.002, AI Supply Chain Compromise—Data) can embed subtle procedural misguidance—e.g., swapping interlock setpoints, reversing emergency-procedure steps, or teaching that certain alarms are nuisance and may be silenced—that trainees internalize as correct. This is **persistent** and **stealthy**: no one notices until months later when a graduated trainee mishandles a real transient. **Prompt injection** (AML.T0051) is also salient: if the tutor ingests trainee questions or facility documents without sanitization, an adversary (or mischievous trainee) could inject instructions that cause the model to teach incorrect scram criteria or disable certain procedural checks in its explanations. The model's persuasive, personalized style amplifies impact—trainees won't cross-check every answer against hard-copy Tech Specs. **Data exfiltration** (AML.T0024, AML.T0057) is a secondary but real risk: if trainees input sensitive facility details (outage schedules, security-plan gaps, or even just which interlocks are 'always tripping') during tutoring sessions, and those logs are accessible or the model's context leaks, adversaries gain operational intelligence. Finally, **cost/resource attacks** (AML.T0034) could deny service during critical pre-exam study periods, but the graver risk is that trainees, having grown dependent on the AI, are suddenly without their crutch and perform poorly or unsafely in simulator or on-shift scenarios.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case embeds an LLM as a learning scaffold for operator trainees, which means the model's outputs shape mental models and procedural knowledge that trainees will later apply in safety-critical operational contexts. From the ML engineering standpoint, the system's fragility lives at the intersection of data provenance (how well do the training corpora actually reflect current procedures and reactor fundamentals?), retrieval fidelity (does the grounding mechanism surface the right procedure or does it hallucinate plausible-sounding but incorrect steps?), and inference-time repeatability (will the same trainee question yield consistent, auditable answers?). The fine-tuning process introduces additional risk: if the model is adapted on a small set of facility-specific procedures or synthetic training dialogues, it may overfit to stylistic patterns while missing edge cases or fail gracefully when a trainee asks about an off-nominal scenario the fine-tuning set never covered. Because this is a teaching tool, there is no real-time interlock to catch errors before they become internalized knowledge, and the human-in-the-loop (instructors) may not review every interaction, meaning skill fade or automation bias can propagate undetected until a trainee reaches the simulator or the control room.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary threats fall into three buckets. If the fine-tuning dataset or the RAG knowledge base is not kept current, the tutor will drift out of alignment with actual operational practice, teaching trainees outdated or superseded procedures; this is exacerbated if the system was fine-tuned on a small, static corpus (OP.C0202) and never re-qualified after procedure changes. Hallucination or procedural misattribution (OP.C0304.01) could teach incorrect emergency responses or security protocols; if undetected, this creates exploitable knowledge gaps an adversary could trigger during an attack. Concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is inevitable as procedures evolve, regulations update, or facility configurations change—operators trained on outdated AI outputs become a liability, and an adversary timing an attack to coincide with known procedural changes could exploit this lag. Small-data/low-base-rate problems (OP.C0202) for rare but critical scenarios (severe accidents, security events) mean the LLM likely has weak or hallucinated coverage of exactly the situations an adversary would induce. If the system is qualified statically (OP.C0303) but used in a dynamic training environment, degradation may go unnoticed until operators fail in the field. Data provenance issues (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03) if training on simulated or transferred data rather than ground-truth operational procedures could embed systematic biases that an insider familiar with the discrepancies could exploit. Finally, the system's cross-site propagation risk (OP.C0602) if deployed across a research-reactor fleet turns a single compromise into a program-level vulnerability, and its cloud dependency (OP.C0601) introduces external attack surface and potential loss of training capability during a coordinated cyber-physical attack.
